maintopic: COPYRIGHT ACT AMENDMENT

speechtext: Mr. L. J. LADNER (Vancouver South) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 16, to amend and make operative certain provisions of the Copyright Act.

maintopic: COPYRIGHT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: COPYRIGHT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
This bill embodies in the main the recommendations of a special committee that was appointed to inquire into the matter and which acted, I think, in 1924.
From time to time the proposed1 amendments were deferred, and latterly the delay was due to the conference at Rome dealing with the Berne convention. It was understood that the government would introduce legislation relative to the convention at Rome, and also dealing with the questions involved in the committee's report. No such legislation has so far been introduced. As this bill embodies the recommendations of the special committee and as there is practically nothing in the bill that is controversial, with the exception of one clause, it is not anticipated that there will be any serious objection in the house by those who understand the proposed amendments.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 15, to amend the Export Act.

maintopic: EXPORT ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: REFUSAL OF RELEASES AND CLEARANCES TO COUNTRIES WHERE IMPORTATION OF LIQUOR FORBIDDEN
speechtext: Explain.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: EXPORT ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: REFUSAL OF RELEASES AND CLEARANCES TO COUNTRIES WHERE IMPORTATION OF LIQUOR FORBIDDEN
speechtext:
The purpose
of this amendment is to authorize officials of the Dominion government having charge of liquor in bond and the granting of clearances to vessels, to refuse to release such liquor or to grant such clearance where the granting of such release or clearance in any case would facilitate the introduction of intoxicating liquor into a country where the importation of such liquor is forbidden by law.

maintopic: EXPORT ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: REFUSAL OF RELEASES AND CLEARANCES TO COUNTRIES WHERE IMPORTATION OF LIQUOR FORBIDDEN
speechtext: Is it entirely in the discretion of the officials to refuse the clearance?

maintopic: EXPORT ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: REFUSAL OF RELEASES AND CLEARANCES TO COUNTRIES WHERE IMPORTATION OF LIQUOR FORBIDDEN
speechtext: I did not catch the remark of my hon. friend, but I gather that he asks if the bill leaves discretionary powers to officials, or whether it is intended as a measure to prohibit absolutely any possibility of export in certain cases.

maintopic: EXPORT ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: REFUSAL OF RELEASES AND CLEARANCES TO COUNTRIES WHERE IMPORTATION OF LIQUOR FORBIDDEN
speechtext: No. I understood the right hon. gentleman to say that the bill left it entirely in the discretion of the officials to refuse clearance, without any government action in the matter. Is that the case or is this a matter in which the government will take action?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: EXPORT ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: REFUSAL OF RELEASES AND CLEARANCES TO COUNTRIES WHERE IMPORTATION OF LIQUOR FORBIDDEN
speechtext:
My hon.
friend will see on reading the bill that the government will take action to prohibit export ; it is not left to the discretion of officials.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to bring in a measure to confirm the agreement between the governments of the Dominion and the province of Alberta, dated 14th December, 1929, respecting the transfer of the natural resources of Alberta.
Motion agreed to, and the house went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

maintopic: NATURAL RESOURCES
subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH ALBERTA
speechtext: I assume, Mr. Chairman, that the agreement will be attached as a schedule to the bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: NATURAL RESOURCES
subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH ALBERTA
speechtext: Quite right.

maintopic: NATURAL RESOURCES
subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH ALBERTA
speechtext: In view of that circumstance, if it is agreeable to the administration we would reserve our discussion until after the bill is printed and let the resolution pass without further delay.

maintopic: NATURAL RESOURCES
subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH ALBERTA
speechtext: I think the committee are entitled to see the agreement in black and white. We do not know how the Privy Council will construe this agreement. We do not want any more agreements such as that made in 1905. I think before the committee is asked to pass this resolution we should have a copy of the agreement before us. Is Alberta to have a law of its own manufacture? Is it to be an extension of the act of 1905? It is well known that a clause was put in that act which was ultra vires of parliament. What kind of agreement is to be made with the province of Alberta in regard to its natural resources-its water-powers, its mines, its forests, its lands? What sort of an agreement is this anyway? I remember three or four years ago when I raised this question in the house, an election was pending, and all of a sudden the Minister of the Interior brought up the subject and announced that legislation would be brought into the house giving effect to an agreement. What happened? I had a resolution on the order paper and it was put at the foot of the list. The government of the day kept that resolution on the order paper for four or five months so that no one could ask any questions about it until the minister reintroduced it. The result was that no one in this house could do anything. I think, Mr. Speaker, every member of this house is entitled to see the agreement and to know what is in it. Is this the way parliament is going to pass agreements, without anyone seeing them? No member on the opposition side at least has ever seen this agreement, and we will be asked by our constituents, how did this agreement slip through the house?

maintopic: NATURAL RESOURCES
subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH ALBERTA
speechtext: An agreement was placed in the box of every member in the house.

speechtext:

speechtext:
Hon. J. H. KING (Minister of Pensions and National Health) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to bring in a measure respecting allowances to war veterans, to provide assistance for certain veterans who are not in receipt of pensions, or wiho, if in receipt of pensions, are only partially pensionable, or who are unemployable, and to provide for the administration, amounts, terms and conditions of such allowances, and for the payment of such sums as may be necessary to carry out the provisions of the proposed legislation.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this will constitute an endeavour on the part of the government to meet an outstanding need in the lives of our veterans, which need has been recognized for some years but not provided for up to the present. I might direct the attention of the committee to the fact that in 1928 the committee on pensions and soldier problems included the following in their return to this house.
"Your (mmmittee finds that one of the most serious situations confronting the department and the country generally is that relating to the employment and care of ex-members of the forces suffering from disability, broken down or burned out. A number of suggestions have been made to your committee for dealing with such cases.	I he committee recommends information be gathered which will be of assistance in framing the government's policy. The committee consider this the most serious problem which has arisen in connection with our ex-soldiers."
Our present pension legislation is specifically designed to compensate veterans whose disa-

Allowances to War Veterans
bilities are traceable to war service, but it has become increasingly apparent that some provision inevitably must be made to provide for the aged and unemployable veteran whose condition may not be directly traceable, under our present legislation, to war service. Recognizing the fact that this is the major problem with which the department is faced I have given the question my personal attention for some time, and for a period of some months have had a committee of the department and an officer of the soldier settlement board devote their whole time to the study of this question. As the result of this review, we have come to the conclusion that in order to take care of a situation which is entirely apart from our pension legislation, an act such as that to be introduced to-day is required for the aged and unemployable veterans.
I .aim definitely of the o-piniion that this new legislation should be administered by a committee composed of the senior officials of the department. In that way, the experience of the department, gained during the past decade will be brought to bear on the solution of a problem which, through lack of adequate legislation, the department heretofore has been unable to handle. Because of this acceptance of responsibility by the government many of the cases which were oited recently in this house will be provided for. Although we have had such cases in mind in designing this legislation, we realized that there were many other types of cases not referred to during the debate which will be covered by this legislation, and thus we will be extending to our ex-service men the best possible consideration within the country's resources. For this reason I am suggesting that the principle of this resolution receive the endorsation of the house so that the committee may have the guidance of parliament's wishes in the matter.
It will be observed that the age of eligibility is set at sixty-five. I propose to place at the disposal of the special committee complete data and information as to the estimated cost of this measure were the age set, for example, at sixty instead of sixty-five.
The legislation which will follow this resolution is the most far-reaching of all veteran legislation so far introduced, in that, for the first time, it recognizes and makes provision for the .man who was discharged fit, who is now unemployable, but who has not been found, under our present legislation, to be entitled to pension. In making provision for the non-pensionable man, Canada will be a pioneer in enacting legislation of this character. It will be seen that we propose to pay an allowance to men with front line
service, or to pensioners, or former pensioners, no matter where their service, at a stated age, provided they are in necessitous circumstances. It is provided also to pay this allowance to men in this class, irrespective of their age, if they are found to be in necessitous circumstances and permanently unemployable Reservations have been made as in the old age pension legislation, restricting the amount receivable from this legislation and other sources combined.
It is not necessary for me to repeat what has been so frequently stated in this house, namely, that many men who rendered splendid service at the front are in need, and have been found non-pensio>nable. It is equally unnecessary for me 'to state that the effects of front line service have had a telling effect on the constitution and work expectancy of our veterans, so that many have aged before their time. This legislation provides for an allowance to these men. There is no doubt that in some cases the legislation will benefit men whose physical conditions are not due to their war service, but if we are to err we prefer to do so on the side of generosity towards those who served Canada so generously in their better days.
I sincerely hope that ail parties and all hon. members will see their way clear to cooperate with the government by endorsing this principle and referring the measure to the parliamentary committee where it, together with other proposals involving the welfare of out veterans, should be further considered.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
There is admittedly a demand throughout the country that some provision be made for the man who is burnt out or who is prematurely aged although he may not be suffering from disabilities strictly attributable to war service.
There is however another matter which the government should work out in detail and submit to the house rather than to the com-

mittee, and that is how we are going to provide adequate compensation to the man who is admittedly suffering from war disabilities but who is not receiving the pension to which he is entitled. Then provision should be made for the man suffering from war disabilities which are not admitted as being attributable to war service. There are literally thousands of these men throughout the country.
There is something wrong with the Pension Act or something wrong with the administration, and personally I believe it is the act which is mainly at fault. The pension board sitting in a stuffy office in the Daly building cannot investigate these cases, they cannot accurately determine whether or not a man in British Columbia is suffering from disabilities attributable to war service. The returned man has not been provided with the machinery to enable him to prove that his disability is attributable to war service. In my opinion that is a vital question to which this house should address itself. Let us ascertain if we have the machinery capable of dealing with this question. I do not believe we have. About three years ago I complained in this house very bitterly about a specific case. I do not like giving specific cases, but I introduced that one to bring home to the house the impossibility of individuals having their cases properly investigated and adjudicated upon. It was the case of a widowed mother and the dispute was as to whether or not her son had been her sole support. The pension board investigated the case from their offices in the Daly building. They refused from 1916- I think it was 1927 when the case was discussed in the house-over a period of eleven years, to grant the man a pension. But about a yqar and a half ago, the pension board, or a section of it, was in Vancouver, and it was good enough to investigate the case on the ground. They heard the evidence and due to complications which had arisen over a period of eleven years, seven lawyers were present at the hearing. After hearing the details of the case on the ground, the pension board came to the conclusion that they had been wrong for eleven years, and they reversed their decision. That is why I ask the government to take into consideration the fact that the pension board is not equipped in the Daly building to investigate and determine whether or not a man's disability is attributable to war service.
The matter has now reached the stage where the pension board should be remodelled. Every case that comes up now is difficult and one which requires investigation on the ground. The man who is disabled and who thinks his disability is attributable to war ser-

Allowances to War Veterans
vice should be given an opportunity of appearing before a quorum of the board so that he will get a square deal. He has not that feeling now. A man 3,000 miles away from the board, may go before his own doctor who gives him a certificate of attributability but apparently no attention whatever is paid to such certificate by the pension board at Ottawa.
A matter of major importance that should be dealt with by the special committee this session is: How are we going to provide for dealing with the difficult cases of men who are suffering from disability and who claim that such disability is due to war service? There are many of those cases and they are not provided for in this resolution. I would hate to think we would have to sit here for months hearing evidence on this point, as we have done in the past, when it is perfectly clear what we should do. We have the machinery and the medical men under the Old Age Pensions Act. Why not allow a soldier, if he is going to get an old age pension, to come under the Old Age Pensions Act and prove to the medical men who are administering the act, that he is eligible because of his position? Let the personnel of the Old Age Pensions Act administer it, the full amount of the pension to be paid by the Dominion government. The machinery is in existence in each province. It certainly can be added to slightly, and the advantage of it would be that the machinery would be on the ground right where the man lives. The medical men could examine him on the ground and determine whether or not he is a man so advanced in age that he could qualify for an old age pension. The matter is only one of accounting. The federal government could pay the full amount that is so paid out annually. It is a very simple matter. Why provide for an entirely new department such as will be provided for under this resolution?

speechtext:
The other day when this matter was under discussion, I was absent due to illness of one of my partners, and I should like to make one or two observations.
I wish to reiterate in the strongest possible terms, the statement of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Clark) that this question should, above all things, be kept out of politics or of any possibility of political influence of any kind. It certainly seems to me an objectionable form of administering a delicate matter of this sort, which is so 
near the hearts and feelings of the people of this country, not to speak of the men who are returned soldiers, that the administration of the act and decisions should be left in the hands of officials directly under the control of a minister or a government.
In that statement I do not reflect upon the present minister or upon any minister, but it is only human nature to expect that he would be influenced by a situation of that kind, and to a certain extent the matter would be beyond his control. I think the house is unanimously agreed that some remedial legislation is necessary at the present time. Grievances have been accumulating throughout Canada for some considerable time, and im my judgment the legislation which is now before the house should have been brought before parliament some considerable time ago. As this resolution is the usual formal resolution preceding a bill, the terms of which are now definitely drafted, disclosing the government's policy, I would ask whether any provision is made in the bill for the widow of a deceased soldier who was denied a pension, but whose dependents under this bill would have received a pension had he lived.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
This enactment
deals with the veterans only. There is a provision that the veteran who is a married man will receive $40 a month instead of the $20 which he would receive if he were single. The legislation, however, deals entirely with the veteran, and it is not proposed by this bill to pension widows or dependents, but rather to provide an amount that will assist them in carrying on during the period when they are in these unfortunate circumstances.
As to my hon. friend's suggestion regarding the departmental committee, it is easy to say that such a committee would be political. As a matter of Tact, we have in the department to-day a very large number of officials who are dealing with cases just like this from day to day. Some 3,500 patients are now in our hospitals. I have not heard that there has been any political influence or any sort of political activity in the carrying on of this work. The reason why I have suggested that this enactment should be entrusted for its administration to a departmental committee, to men who are doing this very work each day, is that their services and the knowledge that they have gained over a period of years and the machinery of the department might be utilized. New machinery, of course, would have to be built up if a commission were

speechtext:
I am very reluctant
to criticise the measure which the minister has outlined, but not having the bill before us it is hard to grasp its purport simply from the minister's explanation. It does strike me however, that this is a radical departure from the system that we have heretofore followed, and one which in my humble judgment, from the knowledge I have, is not desirable. Unless you call it by some other name than pension, it is undoubtedly discriminating between two classes of soldiers, and if I may say so, I think that this legislation is taking away the rights of one class. In other words, it is going to put a part of those who should be eligible for pension practically on the dole in this country. The minister shakes his head. I hope I am wrong, but I cannot see how it will work out in any other way. Suppose, for instance, that you have a pensioner to-day who has been on the pension roll since the end of the war. You have another man who comes up for examination and is found to have a disability admittedly due to the war; this man in the second case will not only be penalized because his pension will be cut down, but the natural rights which should accrue to his wife and children under the pension law will not be theirs.
*Consequently, sir, I submit we are discriminating between two classes of ex-servicemen, depriving one class of their rights and the rights of their wives and children. In fact the proposal looks to me at the present time to be nothing more than an old age dole. The minister, if I caught his meaning correctly, stated the returned man would have
Allowances to War Veterans

to be sixty-five years of age-probably not in years but the equivalent. Well, who to-day wants to wait for their rights under the Pension Act, rights secured by war services, until they are practically dead. That is what it would amount to. If you are going to say in effect that those men to all intents and purposes must be sixty-five years of age before you give them any pension, why, they will all be dead before they have a chance to draw a pension At the present time they are dying at the rate of one thousand a year. I do think this proposed legislation is a misnomer and altogether wrong. I do not think legislation of this kind should be brought in by a government and then handed to a committee with these instructions: Rubber stamp it on behalf of the people of Canada. If that is not the intent, why is this bill introduced at all? If this is to go to a nonpartisan committee as named by the minister, why should not the whole problem be sent to that committee to deal with and to draft legislation in accordance with their views. Why should the government followers go to the committee more or less pledged to support this legislation? I say it is discrimination; it is depriving the veterans, and in many cases the most desirable class of veterans, of their rights under the law. We are saying to them: You have to be sixty-five years of age before you get anything. Then we deprive their wives and families of the benefit which other pensioners get under the present act.
Now, Mr. Chairman, there is no doubt at all in my mind that what applicants for war pensions want to-day is this: they want a fair show; they want their rights; they do not want to be paupers; and above everything else they want some assistance to prove their case before the Board of Pension Commissioners. In the last two or three days I have had dozens, yes, I think probably hundreds of letters, telephone calls and telegrams from people who are in this class. Only this morning a man visited my room and produced a number of certificates from medical men throughout the country certifying that he had tuberculosis. He was asking the Board of Pension Commissioners for treatment. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Pensions will know the man I am referring to. The doctors on the pension board said that he had not tuberculosis; therefore he gets nothing. Now, I am not blaming anybody in connection with this. His own doctor and a number of other medical men say he has a disease which is attributable to war; but the pension board through their medical men say he has not. The man is immediately blocked. Unless he can get support somewhere he is going to be
[Mr. McGibbon.j
deprived of his rights-if he has any. I am not saying that in this case he has. That is the position the applicant for a pension is in. He has neither the means nor the information necessary to prepare his case. A few years ago before the pension committee I moved a resolution that we give the applicant power to employ a lawyer to prepare his case. Colonel Thompson, head of the pension board, stated that this would do more to clear up the situation than any one thing we could suggest. That proposal was voted down. I am not finding any fault on that account. The reason given by some who objected to it was that they did not want to create a class of pension lawyers, and I think there was a good deal of force in their objection. But the applicant is up against a stone wall when he gets that far. The next move is his; all the Board of Pension Commissioners have to do is to sit tight. They do nothing and all the expense has to be borne by the applicant.
If this house is going to carry out the intent of the Prime Minister when he spoke on the address, that we should pension-legally and properly pension-these deferred disabilities, what does that mean? First, that the man has a disability due to war. Granted that, he has a right to a pension under the law of this country, his wife has a like right and so have his children. Take, for example, a case of insanity. Suppose a man entered the war mentally sound, went through it mentally sound, and was discharged mentally sound. Five years afterwards his mental condition breaks down. There is no proof, I submit, in existence, on record, no place where the man can put his finger on as proof and say:	My
present disability is due to war service. And yet there are hardly any medical men or laymen that in very many of these cases will not admit that the breakdown was really caused by war service. I submit that if you are going to reach the class of cases that the Prime Minister referred to, there is no other way in which it can be done except by putting the onus of proof on the Board of Pension Commissioners. That, I think, is the crux of a great deal of the trouble which our war veterans have to-day. My present objection to this suggestion, if I caught it aright, is what I have mentioned, that you are showing discrimination between two classes, cutting off the wife and children of the man in one class and reducing the amount which was legitimately his according to the present law. I shall be glad to study this proposal, but at the first glance I rather think it will not win the approval of the veterans of Canada.

Just one question I
should like to have settled at the present time. I have no desire to discuss the details of this or any other proposed legislation. Were we prepared to study it now in detail, I would see no value in the establishment of a special committee. What I am anxious about is that the special committee shall have the power and latitude, as it always has enjoyed in other years, to take up this suggested legislation and other legislation which is now in existence, to go into it thoroughly, to view it at every angle, and if in the opinion of that committee it is inadequate, to suggest changes in the system by way of amendments to existing legislation so that it may be made adequate to solve the problems which I think we all recognize to exist. That is my idea of the functions of the committee to be appointed, and I am satisfied so long as I am sure that we have that power and that latitude to deal with these problems, to accept suggestions from any quarter, and weigh their merits and bring forth a report which in the opinion of the committee will adequately meet the situation. I have no intention to discuss details now which may be absolutely changed after the committee has scanned them for three or four weeks. That being the case-and I see by expressions of acquiescence on the part of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Pensions that my interpretation of the committee's duties is correct. I am satisfied that with the goodwill of all sides we shall be able to meet the problems that we know do exist, problems suggested by my hon. friend to the right, and be able to deal with them in a way that will be acceptable to the house and just to the returned men.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think it is a misnomer to call it a pension act, or an act at all dealing with soldiers' pensions in this country. As enunciated by the minister in the introduction of this resolution, he states distinctly that the main purpose-and practically the sole purpose-of this legislation is to make the provisions of the Old Age Pensions Act applicable to soldiers when they become sixty-five years of age, or the equivalent of sixty-five years if their condition is accordingly bad. The very principle of the matter is an extension of the Old Age Pensions Act, and I am very much afraid that if we connect this with the ordinary Pension Act of this country, either directly or indirectly- and especially if we put the administration of this proposed pension act under the officers of the pension board or of the minister's department-we are going to find in many cases- cases that we all come in contact with from day to day, of men whose pensions are being withheld owing, as has been stated here frequently, to lack of evidence which is not producible at the time on behalf of the soldier -that they are going to say to the soldier who has a perfectly honest claim for a pension-a pension which should include his wife and children: Well, we cannot give you what you deserve, we know you deserve it but you cannot prove it, so we are going to give you a dole of twenty dollars a month for the balance of your life. That, Mr. Chairman, is what I judge the situation to be, and I think the returned soldiers of this country should distinctly understand the intentions of the government and the probable result.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
It is surprising to have the announcement from the government that the legislation indicated by the resolution now before the house is the only legislation the government intends to bring in at this session concerning soldiers and soldier pensions. There have been committees at many sessions of the house, absolutely nonpartisan committees, and their deliberations have never allowed of any partisanship in dealing with the subject submitted to them- that is, soldiers' pensions and soldiers' affairs -but at the same time, notwithstanding the honest work done by those committees, and the many hours they have put in in listening to witnesses brought from all over the Dominion of Canada, the soldiers' problem is not solved. It must be patent to every member of this house after hearing the speeches made here the other day on the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Muskoka-
Allowances to War Veterans

Ontario (Mr. McGibbon), and the amendment to that resolution, that the Pension Act is not workable, and that it should be amended, re-drafted, and it is the business of the government to see that it is. That is not the business of any committee of this house. It is the business of the minister in charge of soldiers' affairs. What is a government for but to govern, to bring in legislation as its policy and submit it to this house? Why wait -for a committee to suggest these things? Why should not the Minister of Pensions take the lead? Surely he can devise legislation that will meet the situation.
I have heard some hon. members say that they dislike to refer to particular or individual cases. So do I, and I have never referred to one before, but as proof that this Pension Act is not working, and is not workable, I would like to refer to one remarkable case, the case of a soldier named Arthur Murphy, his regimental number being 16392, and I will read extracts from a letter written to the chairman of the Board of Pension Commissioners by the soldiers' adviser of the city of Vancouver, an appointee of this government who does not wish to embarrass the government, but who wishes to carry out his duties in that connection as best he can. I also wish to read a certificate given by this same adviser as late as February of this year. The letter to the chairman of the Board of Pension Commissioners is dated March 18, 1929. He says:
The above noted who is now residing in Victoria, has called on me and has asked that I assist him concerning pension and treatment matters. He has furnished the necessary authority in order that I may peruse his fyle and I might say that I have had the opportunity of examining the voluminous documents and correspondence compiled. I would like to state at the outset that from a dispassionate point of view I do not think that this man has received a fair and just reward.
That is from the soldiers' adviser appointed by this government to the chairman of the Board of Pension Commissioners. He says:
My purpose here, indeed my duty is to ask that the commissioners again review the whole case quite dispassionately and I cannot but think they will come to the conclusion that justice has not been done this man. . . .
It is, of course, a matter of record that he was discharged medically unfit on the 12th of June 1918, and pension at the rate of twenty per cent was allowed for heart trouble and myalgia. This was continued to the 1st day of January, 1922, and then was abruptly cut off, and he has not been on pension since. It is a significant fact, I submit, that the genuineness of his complaints on service and up to the time pension was cut off, was not questioned. . . .
The commissioners, I submit, erred in cutting this man's pension off; there was not sufficient or any evidence to show that the pensionable

disabilities had wholly ceased and determined and certainly the commissioners in their letters to the man were singularly silent as to the diagnosis reached by the several private doctors above referred to. . . .
Time and time again he has been forced to take private treatment and the director of medical services has seen the necessity in treating him as a class 1 patient during these occasions.
Then he refers to the medical men who have given him certificates, and he winds up:
It has been most certainly shown by the board's own officials in this unit that the man is entitled to pension and one can come to no other conclusion than that the refusal of the board is unreasonable and dictatorial.
I do not think, myself, from my dealings with that board-and I have had a good deal of experience-that they are intentionally unreasonable or dictatorial. They are handicapped by the act as it is, and I say it is the duty of the government to amend that act and not to let the whole session go by while a special committee listens to evidence, the effect of which they already know.
Here is the surprising certificate given by the soldiers' adviser at Vancouver on the 1st of February this year, re this same case:
The above named ex-soldier has been now for years endeavouring to establish his disability. He has a great weight of medical evidence in his favour stating definitely that he has a condition of arthritis. Please note in particular the certificate of Dr. Oille, who I believe is a specialist in his line.
And then he gives the dates of the certificates given by twenty-one medical officers, specialists most of them, as to this man's entitlement to pension,-twenty-one different officers, not all of them in the employ of the government:
The ruling of the pension board is that no objective findings have been found to warrant assessment for these under the disability table but it seems inconceivable that the weight of medical evidence in this case should not be conclusive in favour of the appellant. A special board should be asked for to have the case thoroughly examined and reviewed.
We should not be content with the legislation anticipated by the resolution that is now before the committee which is going to extend to some returned soldiers a measure of old age pension, but there should be a bona fide attempt on the part of this government, the members of which and the supporters of which, have at this session expressed so vehemently their regard for the returned soldiers. What the returned soldier wants is not talk; he wants action, and it is the business of the minister and of the government to give it to him at this session by an amendment to the Pension Act which should be brought in now and not towards the close

Allowances to War Veterans
of the session after a special committee have listened for month after month to evidence the result of which they already know.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
To say that
I am rather disappointed in the attitude taken by the government is putting it very mildly. I see in this resolution an attempt to side-step the whole issue in regard to returned soldiers. The minister stated that a man receives an old age pension at the age of sixty-five, and that if a returned soldier were looked upon as being sixty-five at the age of forty he would be entitled to an old age pension. I want to direct the attention of the minister to the fact that at the age of forty such a man has just as much disability, due to the war, as if he had been wounded, and the war is the cause of his aged condition at that time. He served overseas and such service resulted in a change in his physical condition which caused him to age rapidly. [DOT] Therefore he should receive a pension equal to that paid to any other man who received a wound. The whole cause of the condition that exists to-day is the fact that the regulation stated that a doctor must be able to put his finger on a condition in a man's system that is pathological, and say that that condition is due to his war service. Many of these men are looked upon as burned-out and have no demonstrable patho-

Allowances to War Veterans

logical condition upon which any doctor can put his finger, and yet the average doctor knows perfectly well that they are damaged to the extent of a considerable percentage of their normal period of life. The regulations base the percentage of pension on a man's ability to earn a living in the manual labour market. His ability to earn a living is based on the strength and development of his muscular system and the endurance of his heart. Many of those men who grow old early in their lives are unfit to compete in the manual labour market; they cannot compete with the average healthy man, and in consequence cannot earn a living. To that extent they should receive their pensions just as if they had been injured at the war. I wish to draw that phase of the situation to the attention of the minister in order that he may see how ridiculous the resolution is.

Does it not appear to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Pensions that this is absolutely unnecessary? Why should this recommendation be sent back to the same committee, and then returned to this house.

speechtext:
I see no reason for sending it back, because it does not refer to pensions, it simply puts the returned men in the old age list. It simply says this, "We are agreed that having served overseas for four or five years we will take that period off the old age limit and allow you that much for your service, putting you on the same basis as any other aged person." If I am correct this resolution is about two years late; it should have been proceeded with last year. I think perhaps the impulse behind it is the agitation stirred up by Sir Arthur Currie; if so, we are reminded of the promise 
made by the minister at 'Christie Street hospital, when he stated he had an interdepartmental committee considering all these matters. Surely he did not mean the recommendations of past committees which have been accepted and which the government could have put into legislation before this time, but. rather these causes of complaint which Sir Arthur Currie brought before the people in a startling way. If so his interdepartmental committee has not been considering the cause of agitation at this time. Sir Arthur Currie in his letter says:
Our aim must be to see to it that no man who went to the service of his country must be permitted by that country to suffer because of war disability.
The question brought forward by General Currie, and the one before the people, is that of war disability, and this resolution does not deal with that. Some of these men are only forty or fifty years of age, and they would not come under the provisions of this legislation until ten or fifteen years had passed. The men in Christie street hospital were told that an interdepartmental committee would deal with these cases of war disability. General Currie claimed that the time had come for a revision and redrafting from beginning to end of the act, and that has not been attempted by the government. All the government has brought forward is a modified old age pension for returned men. I am not. going to complain because we can never sufficiently reward the veteran for his services, but this is not a solution of the question now before the people. The Prime Minister came to the help of his colleagues by promising that everything would be considered, and it is up to the government to see that the whole act is redrafted and thus meet the Request of General Currie and the Canadian Legion.

apply to the Pension Act at all: it would not be retroactive.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before this^ resolution is declared carried I would like to point out the peculiar position in which this house now finds itself. General Currie wrote a letter to the legion meeting last fall at Regina pointing out certain defects in the Pension Act of this country, and the Prime Minister of this country undertook to-redress those grievances and to ensure that the defects to which General Currie had!

Allowances to War Veterans
directed attention would be met by the administration. In his address in reply to the speech from the throne, the Prime Minister referred to deferred disabilities and to the right of returned men to benefit under the Pension Act by reason of such disabilities. That matter has not been dealt with in this resolution, and there is no measure before the house which deals with amendments to the Pensions Act.
We lawyers have a saying that he who asserts must prove. The onus probandi is upon the man who attempts to prove his case and if there be an equal balance of testimony the asserting party has lost his case. In 1927 we on this side of the Speaker advanced the view, with which I thought the government agreed, that where there was, shall I say, an equal weight to be attached to testimony for or against the claimant, instead of applying the principle of law that he who asserts must prove, the onus of proof would be shifted, as we say, and the benefit of the doubt would be granted to the claimant. The country would have to prove conclusively by a preponderance of the testimony that the case made by the claimant should not be favourably considered. That is my understanding of what was said in the house at that time, and, from what the Prime Minister said in his speech, the country assumed that legislation would be introduced to amend the Pension Act in that regard. At any rate that is my understanding of what was said. The benefit of the doubt would be given to the man who had been passed by the medical authorities as being fit for military service, who had rendered service in a theatre of war, and who was suffering from a disability. That phase of this question had not been dealt with because there is no amendment to the Pension Act. We were led to believe-when I say " we " I do not mean this party, but the country as a whole-that these cases of deferred disability, to which the Prime Minister very properly referred the other day, would be dealt with. These men went to war and the disability from which they suffer did not become apparent until many years after they had left the theatre of war, and it can only be said that but for their service to the state they would not be in the condition in which they now are.
Take the case referred to by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black). Can anyone imagine in a court of law twenty-one medical men testifying that the condition of a claimant was attributable to military service, and one doctor sitting in Ottawa being able to negative the view of those medical men? Is that sound? Is that right? In my judg-2419-17J
ment that is a travesty on justice. The government should have introduced legislation with respect to the Pension Act which would remedy such a condition.
In considering the case of dependents, I will not mention individual cases although it has been done, and very properly so, in the house. Cases have been brought to my attention which make it almost impossible to believe that they have been considered at all by the authorities. When these cases are brought up they point to the language of the act and they say, " Within the terms of the statute we must decline the claim," and I am bound to say that very often they are right in the view they take. That condition should be remedied by amending the statute if we are going to do justice in this matter.
The sole control of expenditure of money rests with the government. We on this side of the house cannot introduce legislation dealing with matters of that kind. I wonder if the house realizes the limitations placed upon private members, members of the opposition, and members of the House of Commons other than the administration, in dealing with the public purse. It is not competent for any one of us to introduce a measure which will increase the pension to be bestowed upon members of the expeditionary force; it is not competent for any one of us to introduce legislation the effect of which will increase the burden upon the public purse. If we introduced remedial legislation to deal with the problems to which I have referred, the Speaker very properly would rule it out of order because we were seeking to do indirectly that which we could not do directly. We are not permitted to submit such legislation, but it is the function of a government to govern, and the duty of the administration is to submit to this house a measure dealing with the Pensions Act, which measure could be referred to the committee.
I had occasion the other day to deal with the case of a widow with many children, who is now a pauper

that is the only word to describe her condition. I knew her husband and I have no hesitation in saying that had that man not gone to the war and assuming that he would have died at the time he did die, he would have left his wife better able to face the future with her children. But owing to his service to the country he was deprived of his earning power for four years. Having lost that, he comes back in health, mark you! and endeavours to reestablish himself. What does he find? He finds his energy less than it was; he finds no sign of disease, but his flagging energies in-
Allowances to War Veterans

dicate his inability to earn the money that he once could. He is passed by and finally dies. He dies from a disease that you cannot say is directly referable to war service. His wife and his children are paupers. This widow's case is one of many in this country and her condition is indirectly attributable to the fact that her husband saw fit to give his services to the state and then found himself, on account of the deferred disability to which the Prime Minister referred the other day, in a position where he could no longer earn money, thus leaving his wife penniless. Are we going to do anything for that widow or not?

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: No.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: I know that is the government's answer, but I think we should do something in that case and I press upon the minister the desirability of endeavouring to deal with such a situation. What is the answer? The government's answer to all that is: Look what we shall do in the committee! In the first place the government has control of the committee; the majority in the committee is a government majority. In the second place, the government's intentions are manifest from the bill they have offered to the house. Those members of the committee who are selected by the government as their nominees are men who, I believe, reflect the attitude of the administration as indicated by the measure submitted. If the measure now submitted had left the financial provisions in blank, one could have understood it; if it had provided skeleton clauses, one could have understood it; but instead of that it makes definite provision dealing with definite matters and provides for definite payments to be made under certain conditions. Therefore, the committee must necessarily be limited in the scope of its activities and in the conclusions at which it arrives.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: Why?

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: Because it is a committee the majority of which is controlled by the administration.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: Is the hon. member suggesting that the members of the committee from this side of the house will not tackle the question fairly?

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
I have no hesitation in
saying that the members of the committee from that side of the house will try to do everything they can to meet the situation and they will do it in such a way as to get the greatest possible political advantage out

of it. The reason why I say that is well illustrated by what is happening in Vancouver. The soldiers' representative in British Columbia is a gentleman who is very actively interested in politics. He sits on the Liberal side in the British Columbia legislature. The other day a scene took place in the legislature in which, according to the report in the public press, he was the chief mover. What is the attitude of men who have to go to him and seek support when they find him so violent in his expressions against Conservatives? Is that fair?

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
He is a nominee
of the legion and the soldiers' bodies in British Columbia.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
The hon. member said
so last year and I saw some exception taken to his appointment by the members of the legion themselves. I point out that as being unfair.
I come to the administration of the legislation now before 'the house. The minister said that there is an appeal from the committee to himself. Is he or is he not a political officer? He is a member of the government, of the cabinet. He is political in his views and in his viewpoints and he is doing what he can in the interests of the party to which he belongs and the government which he supports and of which he is a member. The other day I took up a Victoria paper, and I read a report in regard to certain assistance certain parties were receiving from my hon. friend. It is an open secret in this country that large numbers of letters have been sent to medical men on the pension board. Sometimes they are marked "personal"; they are not before us. Members of parliament have said that as they sat on the Liberal side of the house they could more easily be successful in their efforts to secure pensions than if they were on this side.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: That is very unfair.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
It may be wrong, but my hon. friend knows that is going on in the country. I know personally of cases where that statement has been made. What is going to happen if the minister is to constitute himself a court of appeal, to determine whether a man is to receive a pension of $20 or $40 per month? Do you mean to say that the Minister of Pensions and National Health is not human and is not seeking to maintain in power the Liberal administration of this country? Does he not want to remain in power himself? Is his judgment not going to be warped and biased by reason of

Allowances to War Veterans
that fact, I care not how fair-minded he may be? In a court you can take five experts on one side and five on the other, all men of high professional qualifications, and the live on one side will take a given view and swear to it as their opinion, while the other five will swear to another opinion as theirs. The minister finds himself a court of last resort' under the bill now before the house to determine whether or not people in difficult circumstances shall secure money compensation. Is that fair? Is that right? Is that just? Is that in accordance with the ideas that should be at the bottom of the Pension Act? I submit it is not.
There are two things the government must do. First of all, they must bring in legislation to amend the Pension Act in accordance with the promises that have been given so as to make adequate provision for that class of cases to which reference has already been made, and to which I will not again refer, cases that the Minister of Pensions and National Health knows of quite as well as I; second, to provide a simpler method whereby applicants can have their oases favourably or otherwise considered by the board, and, third, to make it clear that in cases of deferred disability the country is going to deal with them as pensionable cases, and where there are cases of deferred disability the dependents, widows and children who have been left behind, shall have their claims considered by the state. That means amending the Pension Act, but that act is not before the house. If you can dignify the resolution now before the house as meaning anything, it means just what the minister said, an old age pension act for certain types of cases.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: I did not say anything of the kind.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: How did the minister put it?

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: Let the hon. member proceed.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: He has not called it an old age pensions act, but similar to the old age pension provisions.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: Provisions that are apnlicable to old age pensions.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
That means that the provisions that are applicable under the old age pensions will be applicable to cases of this kind? What is the qualification of an applicant under the Old Age Pensions Act? It is pauperism. Under the Old Age Pensions Act no man can secure a pension unless he is prepared to make a declaration in the several
provinces that he has not anything, and if he has any property he has to surrender it to the state before, in many of the provinces, he can become pensionable. Is that the attitude to be taken towards men who have offered their lives to their country? This is not an old age pension. This is not a case of pauperism. This is the case of men who have offered their lives for the state, for men like the minister and myself and other taxpayers. Because we are taxpayers, our duty is to see that the sacrifice of these men is not in vain. That is our duty and that of parliament, and parliament fails in its duty if for a single moment it says it has to deal with these men in a similar manner to the way in which it deals with old age pensioners who have to become paupers in order to get money out of the state. The other day a man said: "The objection I have to the old age pension is that I have to declare myself a pauper if I am to secure a pension". That is a most objectionable thing. Although no pensions are being paid in the province of Quebec, it will require $12,000,000 to pay pensions in Canada this year. What a reflection that is on Canada's prosperity! Now the government is going to add to those pensioners numbers of men who find themselves in a difficult position because they had the courage to leave this country to fight for it. Such treatment is not right and it is not good enough. The Canadian people will not accept it and I misjudge this parliament if it will.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
If there was one note sounded in common by most hon. members who have spoken on this question of returned soldiers' disabilities and matters pertaining to their pensions, it has been that every effort should be made to keep this question out of party politics. We had an interesting discussion a few days ago on certain resolutions moved by hon. gentlemen opposite, and I must say that listening to the speeches that were made from all sides of the house, while much was said of the problem as he saw it from the point of view of each individual speaking, there did appear to be a distinct effort, to avoid making the question one of political controversy, at least at the outset. At the conclusion of the discussion there was a speech delivered which I confess caused me to alter the opinion I had formed as to the object of the discussion. I may refer to it at another time; I shall not do so at the moment. I did not expect that the one person above all others who would seek to make this question from the outset one of party controversy in this house would be
Allowances to War Veterans

the leader of the opposition. I say to my hon. friend that the speech which he has just delivered was a speech calculated to endeavour to make party capital out of this question at the very beginning of the session. Apart from that, the present attitude of my hon. friend is at such complete variance with the point of view which he himself took in speaking in this house on the address, that his speech to-day amounts almost to a complete contradiction of what he said at that time. When we were considering the speech from the throne, my hon. friend stressed above everything else the importance of having this question relating to returned soldiers dealt with by a committee of this house.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
He pointed
out that this was the method by which previous governments had sought to deal with the matter, and he endeavoured to take particular credit to the conservative party for having set an example in that regard. But this afternoon he tells the house that these matters should be dealt with not by a special committee but by the government through specific legislation in advance of any reference to a committee, and he says we are all at fault because we are waiting to enable a special committee to deal with this matter before finally disposing of it in the house. May I read to my hon. friend his words in this house on the 24th of February last, as reported in Hansard.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: What page?

speechtext:
Page 23.
Referring to the speech made by the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Gray), who moved the address, the leader of the opposition said:
We endeavoured in this house-

speechtext:
Not to interrupt, of
course, but the Prime Minister being such a stickler for forms, I would just mention that it is not in order to refer to a past debate.
Mr.	MACKENZIE KING: My hon.
friend evidently knew what was coming.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: I know what is coming.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
I shall not quote from the debate, but will allow hon. members to look it up for themselves, at page 25 of Hansard. I think they will find that the view which my hon. friend has expressed in this house heretofore, if I may put it that way, is that all these returned soldier problems should be dealt with in the first instance by

a committee of the house. May I say that with that view as originally expressed, I am in entire agreement. I believe that the country is of the opinion that that is the way in which the returned soldier problems should be dealt with. I believe also that the returned soldiers themselves, the legion and other soldier organizations, will wish to have this question dealt with by a special committee on which there will be returned soldiers and before which they can appear and make their views and opinions known. At any rate, it was with the hope and expectation, in order not to defeat the very ends we are most anxious to serve, through any attempt, so far as this House of Commons is concerned, to have political capital made out of any phase of the discussion, that we as a government decided to follow the procedure that has been adopted in previous years, and which on the whole has worked very well. I want to make clear that that is the procedure we intend to follow. With respect to any matter concerning the returned soldiers which they individually, or the legion or any other of the veterans' organizations wish to have taken up before that special committee, they should have, and will have, the fullest opportunity to have it discussed there, and the committee may bring before this house whatever report in its opinion should be brought in. The committee in its study of the question will be able to get from every possible direction all the assistance they wish to have, and when their report is before the house we as a government will deal further with the matter.
My hon. friend has tried to make a point out of the circumstance that hon. gentlemen opposite cannot themselves bring in specific measures; that only the government can bring in measures that necessitate the payment of moneys out of the public treasury. I imagine that hon. gentlemen opposite, if one could read their minds, are very thankful that such is the case, because they know very well that of all the questions that arise in dealing with these problems the most difficult is that which has to do with the cost of the legislation proposed. My hon. friends escape the possibility of their measures being judged on that score. If we on this side of the house venture to point out that a measure is going to cost several million dollars, we are immediately told that we are thinking more of the treasury than we are of the returned soldier. So I say that my hon. friends opposite are very glad indeed that under the rules of the house they are not in a position to suggest concrete measures. But there has been no limitation on their suggestions or proposals by way of resolu-

Allowances to War Veterans
tion. They have already introduced a resolution and an amendment, two motions, with respect to what should be done, and I would ask the members who introduced these resolutions if they have ever calculated what the cost of the proposals involved in their resolutions would amount to, and if so, whether they will be prepared, when speaking again to the resolution and amendment, to tell us just how many millions the resolution and the amendment, if adopted, would cost.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: Is that the Prime Minister's objection to it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
No, it is not. I am simply answering my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, who regrets that he has not the opportunity of bringing in any specific measures. I think that my hon. friend from Muskoka-Ontario would himself hesitate very much to bring in any specific measure based on his resolution if he had the opportunity to do it. But I think it is entirely proper that a resolution such as my hon. friend has moved should go for their consideration to a committee of this house on which there are returned soldiers, and before which the returned soldiers can come. I think every consideration should be given to the matter by that committee, and that this house, in the light of the wider knowledge which comes as a result of inquiry before a committee, might well be informed what in the opinion of that committee should be done in respect to a matter of that kind.
My hon. friend has made a reference to Sir Arthur Currie's remarks and some aotion of the government in reference thereto. May I say with respect to the legislation now-brought down, that it was very far under way before Sir Arthur Currie had spoken at all; that the government for a long time has been giving very careful consideration to this matter. Sir Arthur Currie's remarks had reference more. particularly, I think, to questions of administration by the pension board. Sir Arthur Currie stated, if I recollect aright, that there were far too many regulations, that the board was too restricted in its powers, and too rigid in the application of them; that it did not have enough discretionary power, and that in those respects, there should be changes. I think Sir Arthur Currie also stated, in particular, that where there were cases of reasonable doubt upon the evidence before the board the returned soldier should get the benefit of the doubt. I have said before, and I repeat now, that with those expressions of view of Sir Arthur Currie I am wholeheartedly in accord.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: Why are they not carried out?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
If my hon.
friend will just wait a moment: I hope that Sir Arthur Currie, among others, will appear before the committee and give to its members on this particular point the benefit of his large experience and wisdom. When the committee report to the house, having heard Sir Arthur Currie and the officers of the legion and other war organizations, that in their opinion a certain course which Sir Arthur Currie or others may have already suggested should be taken, this house will be in a position to act with a fuller appreciation of what is involved than would be possible without that step being taken in the first instance. I feel sure the country will believe that the government and the house are doing wisely in seeking to arrange to have these gentlemen of wide experience and knowledge in these matters, and those who are primarily affected, given a hearing at the outset.
So far as the Pension Act and its administration is concerned, that is one question, and it will come before the committee appointed by the house and be the subject of the fullest inquiry and investigation. There need be no restrictions, no limitations of any kind upon the extent of the inquiry with respect to the Pension Act as it is. That has been taken as understood from the outset. Right along it has been made clear that a committee of this house would be appointed for the purpose.
But those who have given study to the question and who have knowledge of the situation know that so far as the pension board and the appeal board are concerned they do not begin to deal effectively with what is a very critical and a very serious situation, namely, the class of cases, referred to by my hon. friend opposite, of men who break down as a result of the strain of war service as distinguished from known injury received during, or proven to be directly attributable to said service. These problems of deferred disability, as the member for Muskoka-Gntario (Mr. McGibbon) has used the phrase, apparently do not come within the scope of the present Pension Act. They are not so much questions of the character which the pension board has been considering up to the present time as they are in fact questions of a man's ability to carry on. I mean to say, it is not a question whether or not the disability can be proven to be due to war services, but the simple fact that having served overseas a man finds himself in such a condition of physical or mental impairment that he is unable to earn a living. These cases are the most dis-
Allowances to War Veterans

tressing and difficult to deal with, and we need something supplementary to the existing pension legislation in order that they may be properly covered.
Now, the government might have done what has been done on previous occasions, namely, introduce a blank bill and give it to the committee with authority to consider what in the way of legislation should be enacted. Had we adopted that course probably we would have been told that we had not introduced any legislation at all. In order to put something concrete before the committee-not something that the committee will have to adopt, not something that the committee cannot amend, not something the committee is bound to accept simply because it comes from the government-but in order to put something concrete before the committee which in the opinion of the government should help to meet existing needs, the Minister of Pensions has introduced, or rather is at present seeking to introduce, a measure in the nature of war allowances to returned veterans. If with that legislation before them, and having heard the members of the returned, soldier organizations and others, the committee feel that the proposed legislation does not meet the cases it is hoped it will serve to meet, they may saj' so; if the committee think that that legislation should be amended, they are free to suggest the amendments, they are free to deal with it as they please; but haying something concrete before them, something that has been the subject of much careful study, the committee will certainly be in a much better position to take up this question than they would be without any measure at all.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that the intention of the government in the matter is clear and does not admit of any misunderstanding whatever. In a word it is simply this: We wish to proceed with respect to soldiers' problems, this session of all sessions, in a manner similar to that which has been adopted in previous sessions, in a manner which has been found very helpful in the past. Above everything else we wish the returned soldiers to be heard in respect of any matter which vitally affects them with respect to disability or pension. Particularly do we wish, in the interests of" the returned soldiers themselves, to avoid a political battle on the floor of this house with respect to a matter that is far too serious to be dealt with in a partisan manner.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not grasp very clearly the Prime Minister's idea of what constitutes playing politics. Now, if it is playing politics to endeavour in 
this house to see that fair treatment is accorded to our returned men, then I must plead guilty to playing politics. If the Prime Minister could be with me sometimes when in my office I am called on by men who have fought in the war, and who are now physical wrecks, and if he could hear them tell how they have made their applications for pensions and have been refused, I am sure he would take an entirely different view of our position. I could cite a great many cases where there have been outrageous decisions on the part of the Board of Pension Commissioners, and also cases where I think the board of appeals has not treated returned men fairly. Those men are living in my constituency and they come to me as being their representative in this house. I think it is my duty to do the best I can for them. I have tried the Board of Pension Commissioners many times; I have tried the appeal board many times; I have even gone to the minister and to his medical advisers, I have gone to everybody that I could think of who might have any interest, and I must say that I have received very little satisfaction for those men. There is something wrong, absolutely wrong, with our whole system when a board of pension commissioners can refuse a man a pension, as they have done many times, because the disability in their opinion was either pre-war or post-war.
I should like to read a sample of the oonf-munications which I have received. This has just come to my hand. It is from a man in my constituency who served in three wars before the great war. He says:
Please find enclosed two letters received by me from pensions commissioners, Ottawa, after my last board in Shaughnessy. I may say I have suffered considerably from double hernia and was served out with a truss some time ago. Of course you know I put this down to being blown up in the Ypres salient, 1916. I never received any treatment for this but was considerably shaken up and bled internally for some time after it and not much since I was invalided June 1918.	[DOT]
Although I got treatment for my eyes and ear at the field hospital its always post discharge. If you remember injury arose to my eyes through mustard and tear gas whilst in charge of R. E. Park at Lens Junction and injury to m.v ear whilst in charge of artillery position at St. Nazaire. I was also wounded in the ribs, it was only slight, and stuck a piece of plaster on it and carried on and refused to go to hospital.
My worst complaint is hernia as it affects my carrying on my work on the farm. I know I do not look sick but am very much affected by this. If you remember I joined up at mobilisation. I was to have gone over with the 7th battalion but was sent over on the island on coast defence and transferred to engineers having been foreman in B.C.E.R. car shops in New Westminster. I also contracted in Vancouver for

Allowances to War Veterans
many yeare previously. I was sent over to Prance eventually as reinforcement to 7th company field engineers. Was transferred to 10th company, served twenty-one months with them and C.R.E., invalided home to Canada June 1918. These particulars are to refresh your memory. My son William is getting worse in Shaughnessy and gets very little treatment, for don't think the doctor who is supposed to treat him sees him once in three months. His case has never come up to appeal court.
The letter that he refers to from the Board of Pension Commissioners has the reference S.C.R. 981-F-l., B.P.C. 95968, and it is dated February 3. 1930:
Mr. F. W. Kearsley,
Strawberry Hill, B.C.
Dear Sir:
Your claim has been carefully considered by the Board of Pension Commissioners and they have ruled that double inguinal hernia arose post-discharge. It is regretted, therefore, that under The Pension Act you are not entitled to pension for any disability due to this disease.
Your pension is being continued however at twenty per cent for your disability due to arthritis incurred during service.
That man, as I say, served in four wars. He is una'ble to carry on bis work-

speechtext:
What four wars?
Mr. MicQUARRIE:	I have not that information, but he told me he served in four wars. R'e is unable to carry on bis work on his farm. He .has come to my office; I have seen him. I have known him for years, and he is getting a pension now of fifteen dollars lien- month. I say it is a shame and a disgrace to Canada. A man like that should at least be decently treated by (this country. In the letter he refers to his son William. The boy is in Shaughnessy hospital, I believe a total wreck mentally and physically. He also had some service. After his father enlisted he joined the 131st battalion as a bugler. He got to England, but being too young to be sent to France was assigned to duty in England. He used a motorcycle. He was run into by a motor truck.and was injured. La.ter on he developed very serious trouble. On coming back to England his father saw the boy and was very much struck by his condition. When he left New Westminster he was a strong, rosy-cheeked boy. At his father's instigation, in 1918, having served two years in England, he was returned to Canada, the reason given .that he was under age, and that reason is on his papers. As a matter of fact, he was not under age then. He was undeir age when he enlisted, but he had then attained the age of eighteen years when he was discharged, and he was discharged because
of his physical condition. After his return to Canada toe boy seemed to recover his health a little, and later got married, but since that time he has been going steadily down hill, and at present he is in Shaughnessy hospital, a complete wreck. The doctors at first diagnosed 'his case as sleeping sickness, and they said that sleeping sickness could not be the result of any injuries received at his work. The fact as, however, that the boy is totally incapacitated. There is no dispute as to his being 100 per cent disabled. He is not getting any pension. I understand that the doctors have now changed their diagnosis, and they say he is suffering from paralysis. That family has been badly treated; who ' is responsible? The government is responsible, and the minister of the department is responsible, and I for one am not satisfied that we should have to rely on the department to mete out .treatment to our returned men. Something better should be done for them. I have made the charge several times dn the house .that instructions have been given to the Board of Pension Commissioners to keep down pensions as much as possible, to refuse pensions where they could, and I have actor yet had that denied.

speechtext:
You know very

That is the first time the minister has ever denied it. In any event,

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS

I have many cases,
