maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: In a lump sum?

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
A married man gets more
than a single man.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: How does the minister distinguish in principle between that situation and one where the veteran dies, and his wife and children, who were the cause of his receiving the additional allowance, are deprived of it?

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: It is not provided for.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
What is the difference in
principle? Why does the government make such a distinction and deprive the widow and the children, who received the allowance so long as the veteran was alive, of the allowance when the veteran dies?

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: It is an allowance to the veteran, the man who served overseas, an allowance made when he reaches a certain age, or when of necessity, with the conditions and circumstances surrounding, he has not the means to carry on. maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: Why should not the widow and children also receive an allowance? Why is the proposal of the minister prejudicial to the women? If the principle is one of old age allowance, surely the women and the children are entitled to it; if the principle is one of pensionable disability relating to the pension act, then the principle of the pension act should apply. Under those conditions how can the government exempt the rights of or debar the women and children from participating in the benefits? fMr. McQuarrie.]

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS

Do I understand this act

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
In view of that fact I
should like to point out to the Prime Minister that it hardly agrees with his statement during the debate in reply to the speech from the throne. In his remarks he said-

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: Very well, I will use the Prime Minister's own words; on a previous occasion in {his house he pointed out that legislation would be brought down which would be a modification-he did not use those words, but that is what he meant-a modification of the pension act which would deal with these cases, and said it would be referred to a committee. He was much more elaborate in his pre-description of the legislation which was to come than the legislation itself justifies. This afternoon the Prime Minister said this was virtually a blank bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
No, I said
the opposite of that; I said I might have brought in a blank bill, and then we would have been blamed for doing nothing.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: I misunderstood the right hon. gentleman, but certainly the bill does not justify the pre-description given by the Prime Minister, which dealt very elaborately with it and gave us the impression, if I read his remarks correctly, that it was to be a modification of the pension act. He said that after careful consideration by the government it had been decided to appoint a committee which would bring about what would be virtually a modification of the pension act, so certainly this does not live up to the speech made by the Prime Minister.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
I should like to direct
the attention of the Prime Minister to the observation contained in the speech from the throne:
My ministers have also been making careful inquiry into the workings of the provisions and administration of the Pensions Act with a view to ascertaining what, in the light of past and present experiences, may be necessary to ensure full effect being given to the purpose of parliament in that enactment. As a result your attention will be invited to legislation to make more adequate provision for the needs of the veterans of the Great war and their dependents.

Allowances to War Veterans
That As the paragraph in the speech from the throne which directs attention to the fact that the pension act was to be dealt with, but there is no legislation now before the house; the matter is left to a committee to be dealt with.
The right hon. gentleman referred to the fact that I always have been in favour of these matters being left to committees. That is perfectly true, but when a bill is introduced in this house making express financial provisions, when that bill is sent to a committee, it is quite obvious that the committee is limited by those financial provisions under our rules of government. In other words, it is not competent for the committee to impose upon the country a heavier burden than that contemplated by the bill referred, which is introduced only after having received the consent of His Excellency the Governor General and under certain rules of procedure which have been adopted in connection with such matters. I did suggest and still suggest that a committee is desirable, but not for the purpose of playing politics.
I say that again; I go further and say to the minister that there is abroad in this country the idea that "kissing goes by favour." Let me give an illustration. Only a few weeks ago a widow came to me at a time when certain of the ministers were in one of the towns of this country. This lady asked if I thought it advisable for her to go in person to see the minister, adding that the president of the Liberal association had made the necessary arrangements in the hope that something might be done for her. I say, "Certainly, go ahead," and that has been the case with respect to many matters in this Dominion. If the special committee will consider the matter, have the correspondence brought down and examine the officials, they will find that in a great many instances the pressure of political supporters has been brought to bear for the purposes of accomplishing results. It was to protest against that practice that I rose in my place this afternoon and made the observations that I did.
What is more, the legislation now submitted to this house is the worst piece of political legislation any parliament has had to consider on the eve of an eleotion. What does it do? It puts into the hands of the Minister of Pensions and National Health the power to say yes or no to the applications of these applicants, and if anyone who knows that gentleman and knows what he has been doing in British Columbia thinks for a single moment he will not play politics, he has another thought coming.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
I make the statement
in all seriousness, not because he is worse than anyone else but because he has the great desire to see if he cannot win to the support of this falling administration a few friends among the returned soldiers. That is why I made the observations I did this afternoon. If I felt that this committee was not bound by the limitations imposed upon it by the constitution; if I felt that the Minister of Pensions w.as desirous of carrying out the statements made in the speech from the throne by setting up a committee for the purpose of submitting legislation to deal with the pensions act, I would not have said what I did say. Here is a political officer, a member of the government, who is to have the last word as to whether or not men shall have pensions. Does anyone mean to tell me he will not be subject to the pressure of political exigencies? Who can think so for a moment? Let us look at the hon. gentlemen opposite and ask ourselves if any of them can so think. Is there one of them who does not know what the minister will be doing; is there one who does not know what he will be endeavouring to do when these applicants come and ask for 'his support- on the eve of an election?

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: The same as we always have done.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: Exactly; my hon. friend is absolutely right.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: And we always have done it irrespective of political associations.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: And they expect favourable consideration from the minister whose cause they are espousing in the constituencies. I am not blaming the minister; he and the members of the government are only human, but I say we must not put the applicant in such a position that he has to do what was -mentioned by the h-on. member for Richmond-West Ca.pe Breton (Mr. Macdonald)' the other night. The hon. member gave us instances of cases where men had to make statements as to their political allegiance before they could get jobs.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: Where did that happen?

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
In the constituency of Richmond-West Cape Breton; we were told about it the other night. We also had the situation in Ottawa last year where slips of paper had to be produced in order to get work on the canal. How much more would that be done in dealing with a question of
Allowances to War Veterans

this kind? Let me tell the Prime Minister that in times of stress and strain men who have wives and children for whom to provide, men with very little food in their homes, will not let a small matter such as the question of pledging their political allegiance stand in the way of their endeavours to secure what they need. We must lift them out of that position, and it is not fair to this country to have the minister deal with the question of pensions; it is not fair to those who profess the faith of the party to which I belong. It is not fair; it is not right and it is not just. This committee is hamstrung before it starts. That is the great difficulty; a limitation is placed upon the committee beyond which it may not go.
The Prime Minister asked me why I took the position I indicated. I will tell him; I have taken that position because he has introduced legislation this afternoon which places in the hands of one man the right to determine whether or not the claims of a person shall receive recognition. That is not British fair play, when that officer is a political officer. That sort of thing has been going on in various parts of Canada, and it is high time that practice was stopped. The people who pay taxes in Canada are not all Liberals or Conservatives, and they have the right to see justice done regardless of political considerations. No minister of the crown is the man to dispense justice in such cases whether he be Liberal or Conservative. I want to be fair in this matter; I do not think the members on this side would be the men to do it, any more than the members on that side. It is not right, or just, or fair that it should be done in that way. Let us give these men a chance for fair play. If the sending of this bill to the committee is to be the basis of the action you are going to take, it is not fair play either to the people of Canada or the men it is desired to assist.
The Solictor General (Mr. Cannon) and the Minister of Pensions and National Health will bear me out when I say that in 1927 I was very hesitant to introduce an amendment by which the applicant would be given the benefit of the doubt. The Prime Minister has said that I am trying to make politics of this matter, but it will be remembered that on that occasion seventy-eight members voted for that proposal as against ninety-six the other way.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
Did the hon. member in a recent visit to western Canada make use of that very thing upon the political platform?
An hon. MEMBER; Why not?

Mr. BENNETT; He certainly did, after the Prime Minister had stated that he was going to give the applicant the benefit of the doubt. I stated that his conversion had been deferred because in 1927 he voted against that amendment moved by me, as appears on page 546 of the journals of the House of Commons for that year.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: The hon. member was using that argument for political purposes during his recent visit to western Canada.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
I was explaining the
Prime Minister's sudden conversion.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: You were playing politics.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: No, I was not playing politics-not in Saskatoon; it was not necessary to play politics there. All they want there is a chance.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: You will have to play a lot of politics yet.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: And we hope they will get that chance.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: We will give you a chance.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
I was speaking of the
electors of Saskatoon, but there are many other constituencies which might be mentioned in the same category.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: They will speak for themselves.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
That amendment moved by me in 1927 read in part:
(3) For the purposes of the Pension Act, the disability on discharge of an applicant for a pension who actually served in the theatre of war shall, in the absence of misrepresentation or concealment on enlistment, be conclusively presumed to be attributable to military service.
Among the names of those who voted against that amendment appears the name of Young of Saskatoon. I made the statement referred to in answer to a statement publicly made by the Prime Minister, a statement which he has repeated this afternoon, that in consequence of the statement made by Sir Arthur Currie, legislation would be introduced to provide that the benefit of the doubt would be given to the applicant. That legislation is not before the house.
The legislation before the house is of the grossest political character. If the Prime Minister is desirous and anxious to keep this matter out of politics, then why has the government introduced a bill which cannot be considered except as a political measure, one in which a minister of the crown is to determine who shall share in the benefits of the measure?

Allowances to War Veterans

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend has made reference to a passage in the speech from the throne relating to matters pertaining to the returned veterans and their dependents, and has sought to draw an inference that because the speech from the throne is worded as it is there should necessarily have been an amendment to the Pension Act in order to implement what is there stated. Allow me to re-read the section which my hon. friend has quoted. It reads:
My ministers have also been making careful inquiry into the workings of the provisions and administration of the Pension Act with a view to ascertaining what, in the light of past and present experiences, may be necessary to insure full effect being given to the purpose of parliament in that enactment. As a result your attention will be invited to legislation to make more adequate provision for the needs of the veterans of the great war and their dependents.
Let me draw attention to these words:
-to insure full effect being given to the purpose of parliament in that enactment.
What was the purpose of parliament in the enactment of the Pension Act? I take it to be that parliament expected that any man who had served in a theatre of war, who became disabled as a consequence therefrom, who was impaired in health either mentally or physically, would be able to discover some agency of government which would see that to the extent of his need, he was looked after by the state. In a broad way, I think that was the purpose, that the act was passed with that end in view-that the veteran would receive some consideration from the state which would serve to meet the needs arising from his disability. What has the experience with the Pension Act proven or revealed? It is this: that while there are many men to-day who are broken down as a result of strain during the period of war, they are unable to show that that impairment of their health is attributable to any specific cause connected with the war itself. We may all be prepared to admit that the present impaired condition of health of these men is due to the war, but they are not receiving from the state the consideration which parliament believed they would receive when the Pension Act was passed. The government, having gone into this matter very fully, has come to the conclusion that in that particular the Pension Act does not meet the present situation; the Pension Act does not meet the cases of those men who are breaking down to-day from causes undoubtedly due to service in a theatre of war, but who are unable to link up their disability in some specific and direct
way with something which occurred while overseas. The government has sought to devise legislation which would meet that class of case, but it does not follow that this should be in the form of an amendment to the Pension Act.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: Naturally it would.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: Not at all, it may well be a separate measure. Let me make this statement for the consideration of my hon. friend; I may say quite honestly that it was very much in my mind when we were considering this matter. Rightly or wrongly there has grown up a certain prejudice against the pension board.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: Change it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
Criticisms have been directed against the pension board to the effect that they were too rigid in their interpretation of the law, and that they had become mechanical and bureaucratic in their method of carrying out their duties. Had we as a government brought in an amendment to the Pension Act to deal with the class of cases I have mentioned and which would have referred the whole question to the pension board, wc would have been told at once that we were simply perpetuating a system with which the majority of returned men were finding fault. For that reason we took particular care to prepare a separate measure to deal with this class of case, to avoid any possibility of its being thought that the government was seeking to bind around with regulations and rigid rules of one kind and another the benefits which were to be given under the measure. That is why the present legislation is being introduced in the form in which it is.
My hon. friend speaks about the measure being a political one. He said a moment ago that the referring of it to a committee was political-

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: No, no.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: -because the followers of the government in that committee would be bound by whatever the government said. May I say to him and to the house that I hope every member of that committee who comes from this side will feel that he is absolutely free to deal with this legislation as he thinks best. The government in no way wishes the committee to feel limited as to how far they shall go or what they shall or shall not do.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
Why were not the
amounts left blank?

Allowances to War Veterans

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
Because if
they had been left (blank my hon. friend would have said that we had done nothing; that is why. It is useless for anyone to hope to please hon. gentlemen opposite.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: That is not an answer.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
I said that the man has
to declare himself a pauper to get it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: I do not agree with my hon. friend. There are many receiving old age pensions to-day whom I am sure my hon. friend will hesitate very much to describe as paupers.

maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext: Then, under the regulations they are not properly qualified to get it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSION-ABI.E RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
There is such
a thing as honourable penury which is very different from pauperism. One who receives an old age pension is not accepting charity but is receiving from the state that to which he has a right in accordance with the interpretation to be placed upon the provisions of the Old Age Pensions Act. That was explained when the measure itself was being discussed. As an example, under the industrial system to-day, it happens that many men, through no fault of their own, find it impossible to secure employment after they have passed a certain age. Changes that have arisen in the occupations in which they are engaged, through mechanical or electrical inventions and the like, have left them absolutely handicapped in the race of competition, and they 
cannot get employment. Those men are not paupers; they served their day and generation well and helped to advance the interests of the community and of the country in which they have lived. The old; age pension is based upon the theory that those men in their old age have, through no fault of their own, found their incomes reduced and, as a matter of right, are therefore entitled if restricted in their means of livelihood, upon the conditions set out in this act, to something from the state.
Their situation is parallelled by that of the returned soldier. If a man who has served in the theatre of war comes back and is disabled, whether you can trace his disability directly to some act in the theatre of war or not the mere fact that he has served in a theatre of war should entitle him in case of necessity to some consideration from the state itself. That is the purpose of the legislation which we have brought down, and I repeat that in bringing it down in this form we believe we have removed it from the prejudice which might attach to any amendment to the Pension Act, or to move in the way of administration under the Pension Act. If by any chance there is what my hon. friend opposite says, namely, the possibility of political interference or political control in any form, let the committee amend the legislation in any way that will help to remove that. Our desire is to get this matter as far removed as possible from political control, and our discussions in the house also as far removed from political controversy, as possible.
At six o'clock the Speaker resumed the chair and the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: MOTOR VEHICLES

speechtext: Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Toronto Northwest) moved the second reading of Bill No. 4, to amend the Criminal Code (motor vehicles).

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: MOTOR VEHICLES
speechtext: Would my hon. friend explain this bill?

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: MOTOR VEHICLES
speechtext:
Everybody knows the appalling loss of life that is taking place on the highways to-day. The law as it has been for many years is contained in sections 284 and 285 of the Criminal Code, dealing with what is popularly known as motor manslaughter. The subject of motor manslaughter has been before judges, magistrates and coroners' juries and grand juries many times. In the city from which I come 87 people were killed on the highway in one year, some of them little children, and in some cases the hit-and-run driver behaved in a most cowardly way, driving off and leaving the child on the road. There is an appalling loss of life on the highways throughout Canada. I do not know of any disease that exacts a bigger toll of life per capita than these motor accidents. Grand juries have commented on the matter as well as judges. That able and upright hardworking judge, Chief Justice Meredith, of London, has taken the ground that the provisions of the Criminal Code are too uncertain, too inconsistent, and quite insufficient to meet present-day needs and that almost any amendment might improve them. To the jury he said, that the deaths and bodily injuries caused by highway traffic would be appalling if their frequent occurrence had not made us too familiar with them, and that nearly all these aocidents are the result of some breach of the rules of the road. Not a moment of the day passes in cities without a deliberate breach of the law. Under the present law a reckless driver is very often
let off by the jury. My amendment would strengthen the law. Chief Justice Meredith with his vast experience and capacity for public rights, further says:
And as now nearly everyone is a car owner and car driver, young and old of all sorts and conditions, it is difficult to get justice in even a civil action. Car-driver-jurors have nearly all the speed fever; and self preservation instincts are so strong that they will not be persuaded to decide against drivers who have been no more unlawful than they themselves often, if not commonly, are.
What then is the remedy? I think it should be: make the laws plain and reasonably severe and enforce them; and cancel licences freely.
And at the other end of the matter: Give no licence to anyone who is not proved to be mentally and physically, and from experience and a knowledge of the highway laws, thoroughly capable.
The present section 285 of the code is repealed and a new section substituted covering (a) reckless driving; (b) injuring persons by negligence; (c) failing to stop, and hit-and-run drivers. Clause ID of the bill covers racing and cutting in where there is no room or place ahead on a highway, in a negligent manner, dangerous to others who are driving carefully. The deceased has as much right to live as these reckless, selfish people.
Section 2A says causing death is deemed to be murder. Section 2B provides that a driver who has killed a person shall not drive again for ten years, even though the deceased was partially to blame. In many cases it takes two to make an accident.
Section 2C is a new clause and a new offence, involuntary homicide. Homicide which is not wilful or wanton but occasions death, even though the deceased was somewhat negligent and his negligence contributory to the accident, renders the accused liable if he could have avoided the accident. The speed of the car is a question of fact for the jury and it is for the jury to say if the accused was driving in a negligent manner.
Section 2E was recommended by the chief constables' association at their meeting in Windsor, from a paper read by the Chief of Tecumseh township who asked one of the hon. members for Essex to bring in a bill. Section 2E is as follows:
Any court, judge or magistrate on the trial of any offence under the provisions of this section may upon the application of any person aggrieved and immediately after the conviction of the offender, award any sum of money, not exceeding one thousand dollars, by way of satisfaction or compensation for any loss of property, costs and expenses suffered by the applicant through or by means of the offence of which such person is so convicted and such court, judge or magistrate may require the offender to enter into a bond to the person aggrieved with two sureties satisfactory to

Criminal Code-Motor Vehicles
the court, judge or magistrate, conditioned to pay the amount so awarded, or such sum as may be determined in any civil action, and if the accused does not pay the amount so awarded or any fine imposed, or enter into a sufficient bond for the payment thereof as aforesaid, the court, judge or magistrate may commit the accused to gaol for a term not exceeding one year or until such time as the said bond is duly executed.	_	_
(2) The amount awarded for such satisfaction or compensation, and costs and expenses shall be deemed a judgment debt due to the person entitled to receive the same from the person so convicted, and the order for payment of such amount may be enforced in such and the same manner as in the case of any costs and expenses ordered by the court, judge or magistrate to be paid by the person convicted under the provisions of section one thousand and forty-four of the Criminal Code.
A poor person has to sue the visitor in Ontario and register a judgment against him in the States, and no one can afford all this. The new clause requires a bond on the spot. The person injured or killed has as much right to use the highway as the reckless driver, but even in a civil action it is difficult to get justice against the reckless driver. One of the most callous persons is the hit and run motorist. Some time ago, a poor working woman returning home from Mimico was knocked down while getting off a bus, but the hit and run driver made good his escape. I could quote to the house articles from the Toronto Globe and the Toronto Mail dealing with the appalling number of motor accidents last summer; for instance, there were forty-seven motor accidents during one week-end. These hit and run and reckless motorists are a law unto themselves. Many of them are tourists from the other side and they disregard our laws, but they cannot break their own traffic laws with such impunity. Some hon. members may argue that the provisions of this bill go too far, but undoubtedly it is time to tighten up our traffic laws and bring them up to date as they did in England last January. This is the opinion of the chief constables' association expressed at their meeting in the city of Windsor. I think the provisions of this bill are necessary to deal with the class of person who are responsible for many of our motor accidents. There is murder in the hearts of some of these men; they are potential murderers; they do not care if they kill you. I repeat, our traffic laws ought to be tightened up to deal with such cases. They have tightened up their traffic laws considerably in England, and similar action is being taken in New York State.
It may not be fair to ask the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) to adopt this bill to-

night, but I would ask him to consider it. He has, I know, some regard for the safety of the public. I think the bill might very well go to a committee composed of members from all sides of the house for consideration and revision.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subtopic: MOTOR VEHICLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that the law governing motor traffic should be very strict, but I am afraid that my hon. friend's bill, if enacted, would defeat the purpose he has in view. I may say at once that the government intends this session to bring down legislation amending the criminal code in many respects, and that part of the code relating to motor accidents will be particularly dealt with. Therefore I would suggest to the hon. gentleman that he allow his bill to stand until the government measure is brought down, when the whole matter can be discussed. Then, of course, he will be at liberty to move any amendment he desires, even to the extent of incorporating the provisions of this bill if he thinks they are better than those of the bill which I intend to introduce. These provisions are being considered, and we are basing that consideration on the experience of the attorneys general and the deputy attorneys general of the provinces, who have the administration of justice under their control. My hon. friend in his explanatory note has this:
Under the code now, murder or manslaughter may be charged where the victim dies, in the case of a hit-and-run driver, hut if the victim survives, after injury, there is no penalty except fine under the various motor vehicles' acts and no adequate section of the code to fit the case. The amendments are intended to cover suoh cases.
That is not the experience as it is conveyed to us. I think my hon. friend is wrong in the statement contained in the explanatory note. The fact is that in cases where the victim survives the driver is liable to two years' imprisonment under the provisions of section 284 of the criminal code, which reads as follows:
Everyone is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to two years' imprisonment who, by any unlawful act, or by doing negligently or omitting to do any act which it is his duty to do, causes grievous bodily injury to any other person.
This section is the section under which prosecutions are being instituted when the victim survives.	But the difficulties which
the provincial authorities have had to meet -and more particularly in Ontario-did not arise in cases where the victim survived. It has been in cases where charges of manslaugh-

Criminal Code-Embalming
ter were laid following the victim's death. In those cases experience has shown that it is very difficult to get juries to convict of manslaughter, and for a time it was thought by some of the judges that where the victim died no conviction could be made for criminal negligence under section 284, which I have quoted, with the result that a number of people escaped punishment. We had for a time the intention to amend the criminal code, by adding a section stating that the jury ma}' find the accused not guilty of manslaughter but guilty of criminal negligence under section 284, but we have been advised by the deputy attorney general of Ontario that the first appellate division of the supreme court of Ontario has delivered a judgment in the case of Rex vs. Starr, holding that the crown had a right to charge criminal negligence even though the victim has been killed, and this judgment still stands. But I am considering the advisability of making it still more certain, and amending the criminal code in that regard at the present session.
A further difficulty has developed more recently in securing convictions in manslaughter cases, arising out of motor accidents, owing to a decision of the supreme court in the case of Rex vs. Baker, which adopts the view that some degree of intent, of mens rea, is required to establish criminal negligence in manslaughter. The deputy attorney general of Ontario has asked me to amend the code in that regard and provide that when any person is charged with manslaughter caused through negligence, evidence which is sufficient to establish negligence upon the same set of facts in a civil case shall be sufficient for a conviction of any person so charged. That is being considered at the present time. My hon. friend will, therefore, see that we are considering this matter in the light of the experience of the prosecuting authorities in the provinces, and they do not seem to concur with my hon. friend in their view of what the difficulty is. I would also call my hon. friend's attention to subsection (2E) on page 3 of his bill, in which he provides for compensation for loss of property. I am strongly of opinion that this section relates to property and civil rights, and that this could not be brought under the designation of criminal law.
I reiterate to my friend my suggestion to allow Ijis bill to stand until the government measure is brought down. He suggests that this bill be sent to a committee. If it should be considered that the bill brought down by the government should be sent to a committee then the whole matter might be discussed at that time, but meanwhile, especially in view 2419-18
of what I have stated with regard to the various provisions of my hon. friend's bill, if he cannot see his way clear to allow it to stand I would be compelled to oppose the second reading.

I am prepared to adopt
the suggestion of the minister, that he bring in a bill himself. He has had a good many representations, and I am sure he will bring in a bill that will not be too hard on the motorists but which at the same time will protect the public. I accept the minister's suggestion that the bill be allowed to stand and he bring in a bill.

maintopic: EMBALMING

speechtext:
Mr. J. J. E. GUERIN (St. Ann) moved the second reading of Bill No. 6, an act to amend the Criminal Code (embalming).
He said: I would first of all thank the hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) for having drawn the attention of the government to the possibility of this bill not being altogether in order; nevertheless I think it is well that some consideration should be given to it, and then it will be for the government to act in whatever manner it may deem fit.
There is no doubt whatever that we are altogether too hasty in regard to the disposal of our dead. It has become the general practice that as soon as a person breathes his last the undertaker is sent for. The first preoccupation of the undertaker is to put the body in such a state that it will not decompose, consequently he has recourse to embalming. Embalming, as we all know, is a very praiseworthy and very ancient custom. I think it was brought to a very advanced state by the Chinese, when they embalmed their dead, but with us it has become so easy that there is no time lost before the operation is begun. What made me particularly anxious in so far as this custom is concerned was ax experience I had about a month ago, when
Criminal Code-Embalming

a .patient of mine died of heart disease. I had expected that patient to die, and told the relatives that within a short time death would ensue. A few days later a young man came to my house to ask me to certify to the death of his father. I said, "Certainly; I will go out and view the body," to which he replied, "Oh, I have sent for the undertaker." I said, "I hope he will not do anything until I arrive." The man had died at twelve o'clock and I went down immediately after lunch, ariving there at three o'clock, and found the undertaker in full charge. The family said, "I do not know whether they will let you in or not," but I said, "Oh, .there will be no trouble about that." I went in, and the embalmer had removed the greater part of the man's blood; the body was still warm, and he was proceeding to fill him up with embalming fluid. I have no doubt the man was really and truly dead; if he was not, he was decidedly dead by the time I got there. Death is a very slow process, and people should not anticipate the completion of that process. I could tell you of many other instances. I could tell of a friend of mine who was in the halbit of getting syncopal attacks, a species of lethargy. He used to get into such a state that everybody considered him dead, and one day, while going along St. Catherine street in Montreal he dropped, and the people who gathered around declared him dead. There was an undertaker's institution close by, where he was taken and placed in a coffin. It so happened that this man was boarding in the same house as a physician, a great friend of his; they found the .physician's address in the patient's pocket, and telephoned him. That gentleman was out attending his daily duties, so they telephoned to one of the principal hospitals in the city and told them to send someone to give a certificate of death so that they might proceed with the embalming. It took some time for the doctor to come from the hospital, but a little after three o'clock he came sauntering in. The undertaker met him at the door and said, "I have a body here; I would like to get a certificate of death before we proceed to do anything." They went to the coffin, but the coffin was empty. The patient, looking around and seeing himself in a mortuary chamber, had jumped out of the box and gone home. Just as he reached the door of his home he met his friend the physician who was coming out. The physician was startled and said, "Where are you coming from?" The man replied, "Do not ask 
me." The physician said, "I was going up to give a certificate that you were dead." "Well," the man replied, "I was almost dead, but I did not quite die."
Seriously, gentlemen, these are conditions which sometimes occur and which are decidedly dangerous unless there is some precaution taken in order to delay the enthusiastic cooperation of the undertaker with the medical man.
I may tell you, Mr. Speaker, that it is customary for people who endure severe shocks, such as electrical shocks, to pass into a syncopal condition where all animation is apparently suspended. I have here an account from the superintendent of service of the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company, which employs a certain number of men to resuscitate those who are severely shocked. He referred to the instance of a young man named Ferdinand Lapointe, twenty-three years of age, who was electrocuted at 6.05 p.m. Twenty-five minutes later physicians declared the man dead, but at 7.30 p.m. on the same day they were successful in resuscitating him at the morgue. Unfortunately his condition was so weak that they were unable to keep him alive and the man actually died at 8.25 p.m. Had it not been that these people had been called in this man would have been probably embalmed before he died.
Another more interesting case was also cited by this gentleman. On March 29. 1913, Phillip Terry, sixteen years of age, was walking east on St. Catherine street when, at the intersection of Cadieux street, a wire fell and electrocuted him. This was at 1.40 p.m. He was proclaimed dead. At 2.15 p.m. they were successful in resuscitating him and this gentleman personally wished the boy a happy Christmas on the evening of December 24 when he was leaving the hospital to go home for his Christmas dinner. This, as you will see, was some ten months after the electrocution.
Since I brought this matter up I have found several instances in the newspapers, and I have in my hand a press despatch from Naples, as follows:
While relatives and mourners were gathered around her body before funeral services for Maria Todary, eighty-three year old woman of the village of Fillasodo, she startled them by opening her eyes and exclaiming, "I am cold."
Given medical attention she rapidly recovered and resumed her (usual activity. She was thought to have died from heart disease.
Evidences of the premature funeral were hastily removed.

Penitentiary Act-Mr. Church
In last night's paper there was an account of the death of a man from asphyxia. I have no doubt he died, all right, but at the same time I would not be in favour of having him embalmed right away; I think it would be well to give him the opportunity of dying properly first. It is all very well for us to think of this subject lightly but, gentlemen, such laws do prevail in other countries. In France, for instance, no one is allowed to mutilate a body in any way until twenty-four hours after death; the fact is appreciated that animation may be suspended and that the person may not be completely dead. Due to the density of population in our large cities, especially in Montreal, people are living more in apartment houses where there is very little room and consequently when a person dies the body is removed as soon as possible to some mortuary chamber. I think the old habit of allowing the body to remain for twelve or fifteen hours before being taken to an undertaking establishment is more civilized than the recourse at once to this embalming process. I appreciate that probably this act would come within the jurisdiction of the provinces, but if the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) deems it expedient to rule my bill out of order, which I hope he will not, I would ask that he make representations to the different provinces to have them enact the necessary laws to safeguard society. If the bill is ultra vires of parliament, of course I have to bow to the inevitable, but I hope the Minister of Justice will, in his wisdom, make representations and perhaps at the same time send along a copy of the few remarks I have made in order that his hand may be strengthened in connection with his recommendation to the attorneys general of the provinces.

I would point out to the hon. member that the burden is put upon the undertaker of ascertaining when death actually occurred. The bill reads:

maintopic: PENITENTIARY ACT AMENDMENT

speechtext: Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Toronto Northwest) moved the second reading of Bill No. 8, to amend the Penitentiary Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PENITENTIARY ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Will the hon. member explain?

maintopic: PENITENTIARY ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no criticism to offer of the officials connected with these institutions, as they are doing a splendid work. This bill has been for many years suggested by one of the ablest judges in Ontario, the Chief Justice of the Common Pleas. Grand juries have investigated provincial institutions in Ontario. In Hamilton, two sane men for several years were in the asylum and in one case in York county girls were found without food and shelter, in a dungeon below ground, this being a punishment for some minor offence. The chief justice in addressing the grand jury said:
I am in accord with your views as to inspection of these penitentiaries. Such inspection is in accord with that great principle in the administration of justice which for centuries has been applied and was confirmed by Magna Charta, namely, that the people shall have a large share in the administration of justice in criminal cases.
Whether penitentiaries are well or ill managed they are managed altogether by crown officers; and the management of them is a thing of much importance in the administration of the criminal laws so much that assuredly the people should be entitled to some means of learning for themselves what the crown officials are doing and how it is being done.
The grand jury, representing the people of the judicial district, can most conveniently, and at no cost, perform for the people the duty of visitation.
But one matter of detail I mention, because it seems to me that it should receive consideration.
In some counties there may be five grand juries in a year. Let me suggest that their power be limited thus: say twice a year.
The object of this bill is to put into effect the law of England in similar penal institutions under the Secretary of State for the Home department. We have a capable Minister who has been studying this problem and who is beginning to make some headway. I do not see where any objection can be made to this amendment as this has worked out very well in the provinces and I doubt if our asylums and other institutions would be in the efficient

Penitentiary Act-Mr. Lapointe
condition they are in to-day were it not for the supervision by the municipal and provincial authorities, the superior court bench, the county court bench and the grand jury. I do not know whether or not the minister will support this bill but when Sir Lomer Gouin was minister he promised to look into the matter and said it was most important.
The object of section 1 is to give jurisdiction to the grand jury to visit these institutions and to examine into complaints made, and make presentments without expense to the country. These institutions are manged by the crown, and it is the intention of the bill to afford the people some reliable and definite knowledge of the conditions that prevail in them.
I have letters from two gentlemen-I will give their names if desired-who visited one of these institutions and found tubercular men who had not been allowed out in the fresh air. They found the accommodation to be against all the laws of hygiene. One of the government members in this house from Montreal island two or three years ago presented a resolution which called attention to the fact that all the laws of hygiene were being violated in these institutions in the accommodation provided. A great deal of progress has no doubt been made in the good work which the minister and his predecessors have been doing. The grand jury can do this work without expense to the country. The members of the house and others have not time to go into these details, but that is the duty of the grand jury. I was looking up the textbooks, and I find that from time immemorial one of the functions of the grand jury has been to look after good government and respect institutions in the king's name and the respect for the law that they have in the old country has been due to the good work of grand jury. Grand juries have done wonderful work in this country as well.
As regards another clause of the bill there has been considerable criticism in the press of Ontario about a young man in trouble who had stolen a few hens and chickens in the city of Hamilton and was sent to Kingston. The family lived in Hamilton for many years, and this was the first time one of them had got into trouble. The judge, in order to put a stop to chicken stealing, perhaps went further than he intended. The father was sick with pneumonia, and died calling for a visit from his boy. The war has changed public opinion in many ways, and the Red Cross has been doing wonderful work of reformation in the country. There are many

people in trouble who would not be were it not for present economic conditions. Just the other day at Washington, Mr. Willard, president of the Baltimore and Ohio Railway, was giving evidence on unemployment before Mr. Hoover's special committee, and he called attention to the large number of first offenders in these institutions to-day. He said:
It is a dangerous thing to have a large number of unemployed men and women-dangerous to society as a whole, dangerous to the individuals who constitute society when men are willing to work and able to work and want to work are unable to obtain work. We need not be surprised if they steal before they starve. Certainly I do not approve of stealing, but if I had to make a choice between stealing and starving I would surely not choose to starve, and in that respect I do not think I am much unlike the average individual.
I just give this illustration to show that I think an exception should be made in the Hamilton case. The minister's officials said no one was ever allowed out to attend his parent's funeral. Rev. Mr. Vipond wrote a long letter to the Globe in regard to the matter. He said that a prisoner by the name of Shortis, a murderer and a lifer, was allowed out to attend somebody's funeral in Toronto. Perhaps the minister may think clause 2 goes too far because in some cases it might not be advisable for the father or mother to see the prisoner. The third clause has been before the house for some years. Five years ago there were seventy-five, sixty-two and sixty-one prisoners a year of the age of fifteen, sixteen, seventeen and eighteen respectively in these institutions. The minister has been carrying out a promise made to establish two juvenile institutes and has been doing good work in this connection. He has brought forward some very good votes for two institutions that I think will be a credit to the minister in the years that are to come, but he must admit that it will take two or three years to get these institutions going in Quebec and Ontario. In the meantime there is no place to keep these children. I think the minister might take that into consideration in studying the case, and adopt the clause that no one under nineteen is eligible to be housed in one of these penitentiaries.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PENITENTIARY ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The first section of the bill of my
hon. friend would authorize the grand jury of any county in which a penitentiary is situated to visit, view and inspect the same, and make such inquiry as it may deem proper into the state, condition and management thereof, the nature and efficiency of its accommodation, the employment, training and treatment of convicts, the conduct of its officers,

Allowances to War Veterans
prisoners and employees, and of all others having dealings of any kind or in any capacity with such penitentiary, and to examine and inspect the accounts, vouchers, records and books of the penitentiary; and the grand jury may thereupon make such findings and presentments as it may deem to be required in the public interest.
May I point out that such an inspection of a penitentiary as is proposed by this bill would occupy the activities of a grand jury working ten hours a day for several months? May I also mention the fact that the grand juries are composed of excellent men indeed, but they are men with no especial experience in criminology or the handling of criminals, or the management or care of such institutions. Moreover, grand juries are selected and appointed by provincial governments and they have therefore no authority whatever in Dominion government institutions. Penitentiary officials are not permitted ,to inspect provincial institutions, nor is it considered1 desirable that this should be so, notwithstanding the fact that there are confined in mental diseaser hospitals of the various provinces a number of inmates of penitentiaries, the care and maintenance of whom are paid by the Penitentiaries branch. There is already in the penitentiary law all that is required in the matter of inspection. Penitentiaries are inspected in detail by the superintendent, three inspectors, the auditor, the parole officer, the chief penitentiary engineer and the structural engineer. Such inspections are made continuously throughout the year. In addition to that, the following persons are entitled to visit and inspect a penitentiary during business hours: the Governor General of Canada, although I admit that he does not avail himself of that opportunity; the lieutenant-governor of any province of Canada; any members of the King's Privy Council of Canada, any member of any executive council of any of the provinces, any member of parliament of Canada and any judge of any court of record in Canada or in any of the provinces; and such inspection is invited.
May I say in that regard that the condition and the management of our penitentiaries have been favourably commented upon, indeed have been commended by visitors from other countries connected with various organizations, the judiciary or the police forces, and that our penitentiaries compare favourably with such institutions in any other country in the world?

maintopic: ALLOWANCES TO WAR VETERANS
subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSIONABLE RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
I should like to make a few observations on the resolution introduced this afternoon by the Minister of Pensions and National Health, and which reads as follows:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure respecting allowances to war veterans, to provide assistance for certain veterans who are not in receipt of .pensions, or who, if in receipt of pensions, are only partially pensionable, or who are unemployable, and to provide for the administration, amounts, terms and conditions of such allowances, and for the payment of such sums as may be necessary >to carry out the provisions of the proposed legislation.
As hon. gentlemen are aware, .this resolution was discussed this afternoon, and a good many members expressed their opinions as to its effects. An explanation was given by the minister of pensions, and as near as I could gather, the proposed legislation, outside of providing for those veterans who do not qualify under the present legislation, is applicable only when the veteran reaches the age of sixty-five or becomes unemployable before that age through illness.
Three years ago in this house I asked the following questions of the minister of pensions :
1. Will legislation be introduced at this session of parliament providing relief for disabled and partially disabled war veterans at present excluded from pension benefits owing -to existing regulations?
2.	If so, when will the bill be introduced for the said purpose?
I pressed that question on many occasions during that session, and eventually the minister promised to give consideration to the matter and to see what could be done to relieve these cases. I had in mind at the time one or two cases which I shall mention very briefly this evening, and I hope that something may be done to provide relief for such cases.
Allowances to War Veterans

First is the case of Charles Dauphinee, a young man who had enlisted in 1914. He was found to have defective feet and that an operation would have to be performed before he cotdd be accepted for service. He was very anxious to serve his country at the front and submitted to the operation, paying all his hospital expenses outside of the surgical operation. He went to the front and returned in 1918. Shortly afterwards he developed pulmonary trouble and underwent examination by medical experts in the province of New Brunswick. They pronounced his case to be of a tubercular nature and he was ordered to the hospital. Being too proud to accept anything from the pension board, and not desiring in any way to embarrass his family, he went on paying his own expenses as long as his money lasted, but eventually he had to appeal to the pension board. Before resorting to this means of getting assistance he had undergone considerable privation. The board rejected his application. He then appealed to the soldiers' official representative at Fredericton, and he was told that his case seemed to be a deserving one. He was unable, however, to impress the Board of Pension 'Commissioners. He was placed in hospital. First he tried to get into the Newcastle hospital in New Brunswick or into the Jordan Memorial Sanatorium at River Glade, but he was refused admission owing to the advanced stage of the disease. Finally, on November 28, 1929, he died in the public ward in the Lancaster hospital at St. John. I say that in a case of that kind this government should feel responsible for that young man's death. Here was a case where the pension board had every knowledge of that man's condition, and why they did not appeal to the minister, or if they did, why the minister did not bring down legislation to take care of this and similar cases, I cannot understand. Why wait three years to bring down the legislation? I question indeed if the legislation to be introduced would cover such a case. I do not know, but I do say that the relatives of this man who provided the wherewithal to place him in the hospital, and went to the expense of clothing him and providing for him, should be recompensed by this administration.
Another case was that of Private George Weldon, a middle aged man, who passed the physical examination, enlisted and went to the front. On his return he was found to be suffering from arteriosclerosis. The department was unable to prove that he did not contract it during -the war, and the soldier himseJif was unable to prove that he was not afflicted with this disease when he entered the army, owing to the examiner's death.

This man has a wife over seventy years of age. H'e is -now practically useless; his nerves are broken down as a result of his war experience, and he is suffering from other ailments. The legislation which -the minister proposes to bring down should cover cases of that kind where the soldier has dependents of an advanced age.
I want to say a word or two with regard to the official soldiers' advisors. I believe these men intend to do the right thing, but they come into -contact with so many deserving cases throughout the country that it has a tendency rather to harden them against the men who are appealing to them. I should like to quote a paragraph from a letter which an official soldier advisor sent to a soldier a short time ago, to give you an idea of what I mean. He writes:
The only way to establish your case is to obtain certificates from the doctors who treated you since that time and possibly declarations to prove the existence of your trouble as soon as may be after discharge. You will have to obtain this evidence yourself.
I do not see why this man should not have been given -the opportunity of coming before the appeal boat'd, which travels around the country. I do not know how frequently -the appeal boa-rd visits the other portions of Canada, but they have held only two sittings in the maritime provinces, I understand, in the last year. Under those circumstances, to whom are these soldiers going to appeal? They h-ave not the money to come all the way to Ottawa. The minister knows that there are thousands and thousands of deserving oases, and I appeal to him to make his act broad enough to cover all such oases, giving the -benefit of the doubt to the soldier in every case, and leaving the burden of proof on the department. It seems a picture of black ingratitude-*

subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PENSIONABLE AND NON-PENSIONABLE RETURNED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
I should like to make one or two observations with regard to this resolution, which is supposed to give effect to the demand of public opinion throughout Canada from Halifax to Vancouver, and which has come to a head particularly during the last twelve months.
This resolution states that it is expedient to bring in a measure respecting allowances to war veterans, which measure, I presume, will be a government, bill. In my humble judgment we are starting out in the wrong way, for the bill no doubt will be sponsored by the Minister of Pensions and National Health. By the way, what has the minister to do with pensions? Have we not a separate non-political, non-ministerial board of pension commissioners to deal with pensions? Why does this government create a department and call it the ministry of .pensions? No doubt the- purpose is to direct the attention of those who are entitled to pensions to the fact that if they would be in the good graces of those who are in a position to grant pensions, they had better line up with those who sit to the right of the Speaker.
Now, let me put myself right in this respect. I would be the last one in this house, Mr. Chairman, to raise political issues when dealing with a matter of this kind. I would rather lose ten thousand votes in my constituency than by introducing party politics embarrass the position of those men who served us so well during the trying years of the war, but in passing I would say that the title of "Minister of Pensions" was originated by this government.
But to get back to the bill under discussion. The minister will sponsor the bill, his department will administer it and will draft the regulations incident to its administration. The officials in that department are the very people who drafted the orders in council dealing with our returned men, which, as all Canada knows, have not been very satisfactory in their operation. That is not what the great body of our citizens want at this time. They want the Pension, Act so amended that not only the war veterans mentioned in the second line of this resolution will be looked after, but also members of the expeditionary force in general. They want some blood put into the Pension Act, they want to keep it alive, they want to see to it that the men who did so much for us and their dependents will be given real consideration. What should be done to effect this purpose? First of all, get the Pension Act out of the hands of the Minister of Pensions, get it away from the administration
altogether and put it in the hands of the Board of Pension Commissioners. We must see to it that the Pension Act is broad enough and general enough in its scope to carry out the wishes of the people of Canada. They are keenly interested in the welfare of the men who were in the front line trenches in France. They desire that those men should be given full consideration, not in proportion to the consideration given to the men who never left Canada but consideration commensurate with the meritorious service which they gave to their country. As the Pension Act stands now the man who enlisted but did not leave Canada receives the same consideration as the man who served in the front line trenches for the three months.
In the third line of the resolution we find the words "or who, if in receipt of pensions, are only partially pensionable." What is there in the Pension Act to-day to take care of that great, body of ex-servicemen who on their return home find themselves with a ten per cent disability and unable to continue in the vocation for which they were trained before the war? I am thinking of one case now. I will not cite the many other eases in my constituency-a constituency, by the way, which will compare very well in the matter of war service with any other constituency in the Dominion. The man I refer to was a motor truck driveT before he enlisted, but now he has shrapnel in his -back and can no longer sit behind the wheel of his truck and bump along the road; consequently he has to find another job. His disability is adjudicated ten per cent. As a motor truck driver he was able to earn considerably more than the unskilled labourer, but the pension awarded to him is based on the amount of his disability as though he were an ordinary labourer. Provision should be made in the Pension Act to take care of this class of cases.
After listening to the discussion of thi3 resolution this afternoon I feel it desirable to direct the attention of the house to the fact that we have not only to consider members of the legion, but also the men of the amputation association, the army and navy veterans, the imperial ex-service men, men of the air service, and those who lost their eyesight during the war. Not only have we to consider the representations made by these organized1 men, but we must consider that great body of ex-servicemen, representing about seventy-five per cent of our returned men who belong to no organization whatsoever, and are rehabilitating themselves in civil life in their own quiet way; but as one year sue-
2S0
Allowances to War Veterans

ceeds another find that some accident or illness that happened to them overseas is beginning to affect their health. But there is nothing on their medical sheet to show what that trouble is. They find themselves unable to carry on their vocation in their efforts to re-establish themselves in civil life. As I say, they belong to no organization, and are out of touch with the efforts that the legion and the other service organizations are putting forward on behalf of returned men. This great body of men will have to appeal to somebody for consideration. Must they be forced to come to this government for help? -a government which is in office solely by reason of the partisan activities that they are able to employ throughout the length and breadth of the country,-or are those men to be given an opportunity to appeal for justice to a non-partisan body such as the Board of Pension Commissioners? No politics? Why, this is one of the most serious questions that Canada has to face to-day, but, I submit, no party politics should be injected into it. Does party politics enter into the work of any government department? Last Sunday a young man met me on the street. I asked him how things were going. He replied:	"Fine. I
am working in the Post Office department, but last week a funny thing happened. A man came to me and said, 'If you want to hold your job you had better sign this membership card and pay fifty cents into the Liberal association of the city.' " God forbid that that condition should ever get into the Department of Pensions and National Health. But it will be there, if this bill passes and is permitted to take the place of amendments to the Pension Act. I think I would be safe in saying that the Board of Pension Commissioners handle eighty or ninety per cent of the cases that eventually receive pension, and the federal appeal board the remaining ten or twenty per cent. The Board of Pension Commissioners sit here at Ottawa, and pass on the eighty or ninety per cent of the case? through correspondence, and the ten or twenty per cent are passed on by a travelling board who probably do have an opportunity of getting in touch with the man or dependent who is receiving the pension. That, in my opinion, is not a fair deal to the pensioner. The cart is before the horse, and the positions should be changed.
I would like to make one or two further observations with regard to the conduct of the Federal appeal board. Oh, it is nice to see them sitting up there as judges, and it is very nice indeed to have someone represent the man. It is also nice for them to

have three or four secretaries when these ex-service men or dependents, a lot of them broken in spirit and unaccustomed to appearing before tribunals, go to the door, tap on it, with a secretary shooing them into a corner, and lining them up as I have seen them lined up on one occasion, some twenty or more, waiting their turn to appear before the board. And, as I stand here, I can visualize ,a woman in widow's weeds, trembling at the very thought of the cross-examination that is being conducted by the members of the board. The whole atmosphere is that of a court. The man or woman feels that he or she is on trial. I have in mind an observation made to me some few minutes after I had had the pleasure of appearing before this board. A man said to me: "I did not feel that I had a friend in the world inside there until you happened to come in." I bring this to the attention of parliament for this particular reason: the whole machinery for the conduct of this important matter is of such a nature that it does not carry out the mandate, I would say, of the people of Canada in the sympathetic administration of the Pension Act. The people are demanding that every possible consideration be given to these men and women and to see that nothing partisan of any nature whatsoever is introduced that will make it difficult for them to receive proper consideration. One hundred million dollars is being spent by the Edited States on pensions for their ex-service men. This government is spending many hundreds of thousands of dollars to-day sending ambassadors to the four points of the compass. Cut out your nonsense overseas and elsewhere, nonsense that is characterized by brass aind frills, and give more attention to those who are amongst us at this time; see to it-not only for their good but for the good of the generations which are to come-that men looking back into history will say that we did what was right by those who served us at a time when we most needed them.

If dairying is to succeed in Canada it must be carried on throughout the entire year, and if it is to be carried on in this way the Canadian dairyman must receive a higher price for his products in the winter time than he does when his cattle are an the grass. This act is not only recognized but acted upon by the producers as well as the dairy companies and others who are engaged in the distribution of milk in our towns and cities. The fact that butter enters the country very freely during the winter months has had a depressing effect upon winter dairying in Canada. Many farmers have been compelled to go out of the business. These are the words of the National Dairy Council in the brief which, as I have already mentioned they presented just a short time ago to the tariff board:
The combined effect of the actual and obvious lowering of the winter price of butter and the effect of large importations has tended first to decrease winter dairying and, second, to prevent the make of butteT from increasing in proportion to the demand.
In fact the production of butter has fallen off in Canada to such an extent that if we arc to meet our requirements in butter, it would mean that at the present average rate of production per cow, nearly 140,000 more cows would have to be kept. This seems to be conclusive evidence that there is a close relationship between the imports of butter and the falling off in our dairy herd population.
Another very important industry which has been affected by the butter situation is the hog industry. There is always a very close relationship between these two industries. Skim milk and whey, which are by-products in the manufacture of butter and cheese, are very profitably fed to hogs, as every farmer knows. It seems strange, yet it is only natural, that from the very day butter began to flow freely into Canada our exports of pork and pork products began to fall off. In the fiscal year 1925-26 our exports of pork and products, including lard, amounted to a little over $27,000,000, but in the year 1928-29 these exports declined to $9,981,000, a decrease of over 60 per cent. The dairy industry and the hog industry, as I have already said, are very closely allied, and a tendency to lessen our production of dairy products will ultimately reflect itself in a lower production so far as the hog industry is concerned. Indeed I may
say that the foundation of the whole mixed farming industry of Canada is dairying. In all the provinces the average farmer, while producing other lines of farm products, produces a considerable quantity of milk as well. It takes many years properly to equip a dairy farm, to build up a dairy herd, and to put production on a paying basis. After this is accomplished, the success of the industry depends very largely upon the stability of the market and upon the prices which the farmers receive. Production must continue the year round. The successful dairyman is the one who gets the limit of production from his animals, and this can only be done when his cows are milked through the whole period of lactation. If dairy products are to continue coming into this country during the winter months from countries where butter is being produced under summer conditions the year round, the dairy farmer will find it increasingly difficult to operate at a profit.
I have already given figures to the house showing how the hog industry has suffered during the past few years and how the dairy industry has suffered during the same period. At the same time we are continually increasing our imports of frozen lamb and mutton from countries whose products are coming into Canada under special privilege. As an example, there was imported into Canada during the fiscal year 1926, some $2,725,000 oi farm products. This is under the special agreement with New Zealand. In the year 1929 there was imported $14,987,000 of farm products.
