I have given the house figures which I think demonstrate quite clearly that there has been a steady encroachment upon the Canadian market by foreign agricultural products, and that there has been a steady falling off in our production both of milk and of pork products. That the dairy industry is in a grave condition is acknowledged by everyone who is acquainted with the facts. Our dairy herds are being depleted. Foreign agricultural products are finding ready access to our markets. Agriculture in this country is labouring under great difficulties, much of which have been brought about by foreign competition, and this foreign competition is largely due, I believe, to the action of the present government in respect to their trade treaties.
To my mind the remedy is very simple. Measures should at once be taken by the government to assure the full benefit of the home market to the Canadian producer. I have always believed in trade within the empire. I cannot conceive of anything which will bind the different parts of the empire more closely together than mutual trade relations, but concessions in other markets than our own which are purchased at the expense of another industry in this country, and an important industry, may be bought too dearly. Our concessions to New Zealand have gone far towards ruining our daily industry, which has received a set-back from which I believe it will take years to recover. Something must be done before it is too late. Last year the situation was considered to be so serious that a debate was staged in the house on the question. I had the pleasure at that time of drawing to the attention of the house and the government the needs of Canada in this direction. The government was urged to negotiate with New Zealand for a more favourable trade arrangement. When I spoke at that time I did so with the full endorsation of my leader and of my colleagues. The late minister of finance sought to justify the agreement as it existed, and as a consequence nothing has been done. I believe that the Prime Minister, speaking in Woodstock on September 23, 1925, promised the farmers of Oxford county that their interests would be protected in the matter of trade treaties; he used words to that effect. I am wondering at the present time why no action has ever been taken. Surely the Prime Minister and the government are convinced at this time, in view of all the representations that 
have been made not only from this side of the house but from farmers' organizations all over the Dominion, that this treaty has had an adverse effect upon the agricultural industry in Canada. To restore to the farmers of Canada a more secure position in their home market, and as a first step towards that end, I beg to move, seconded by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe), in amendment to the motion which is now before the house:
That all the words after the word "That" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"in the opinion of this house, order in council No. 1757, passed on the 26th day of September. 1925, respecting certain trade arrangements with the Dominion of New Zealand, should be rescinded forthwith, and immediate steps taken to negotiate a treaty with that Dominion on fair and equitable terms."

maintopic: PROPOSED CANCELLATION OP SPECIAL AGREEMENT WITH NEW ZEALAND AND NEGOTIATION OF TREATY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a point of order. I submit that the wording of this amendment is out of order, inasmuch as it conflicts with a rule of this house which I shall presently quote. That rule declares that on an occasion of this kind an amendment must not contain matter relating to any subject which has been already dealt with or which is now on the order paper. I direct your attention, sir, to resolution No. 21 standing in my name:
That, in the opinion of this house, six months' notice should be given to the New Zealand government to cancel the application to that country of the provisions of what is generally known as the Australian treaty.
I gave notice of that resolution on February 24th, so that it was quite impossible for me at that time to have foreseen the action of the hon. gentleman to-dav, and it proves that my motion was bona fide and could not have been designed with any intention of preventing him from moving his amendment.
I submit that the amendment now submitted by the hon. member is a plagiarism, a pale, pink copy, but still a copy, of my motion.
Now, to deal for a moment with the rules. First, I refer to Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Fbrms, second edition. At page 149 he deals with this specific question as to the Speaker's leaving the chair for the house to go into committee, and says:
Neither the discussion nor the amendment, if one is moved, shall relate-
I ask you, sir, particularly to note those words. The rule says:
-the amendment shall not relate to any decision of the house during the current session, nor to any item of the estimates, nor to any resolution to be .proposed to the committee of ways and means, nor to any matter placed on or whereof notice has been given in the order paper.

Australian Treaty-Mr. Neill
Leaving out the unnecessary matter the rule reads:
The amendment shall not relate to any matter placed on the order paper.
So much for Beauchesne. Next I refer you, sir, to Bourinot, fourth edition, page 420, on the same subject of the Speaker leaving the chair. Bourinot says:
The ordinary rules of debate are applicable on this occasion; for instance, a matter already decided by the house, or of which notice has been given, or which stands upon the orders of the day, cannot be discussed;
"Cannot be discussed." Then I desire to cite another authority upon which we rely so much, May's Parliamentary Practice, thirteenth edition, page 526, where practically the same language is employed:
The ordinary rules of debate are applicable on this occasion. For instance, a matter which should be considered upon a substantive .motion, or which has been already decided by the house, or of which notice has been given, or which stands upon the order paper cannot be discussed.
That, surely, is conclusive. I think it will be allowed that that point at least has been established.
Now, to use the language of Einstein, I come to the question of the relativity of the amendment to my motion. Surely it is apparent that we are both dealing with the same matter. It is true the ihon. gentleman opposite proposes to deal with it in a different way from what I do; he is destructive, he wants to condemn the government and play *politics; I want to be constructive, and to have something done that will benefit the dairy industry. We are each dealing with the same matter in a different way, but we both deal with it.
Now I wish to draw attention to the amendment. The hon. gentleman has extended my resolution somewhat. After the New Zealand treaty has been done arway with he proposes that:
Immediate steps be taken to negotiate a treaty with that Dominion on fair and equitable terms.
It might therefore be argued that that extension of action, so to speak, constitutes the amendment a separate and distinct resolution or motion, and consequently that it does not conflict with mine. But, sir, you will readily see that if we allow that logic, then our rules are of no effect whatever, because it would always be possible to copy, we will say, my resolution word for word, and only add a few words at the end proposing further action, which would then make the amendment in order. For instance, suppose my motion had proposed to hang a man,
and the hon. gentleman opposite had proposed to hang and bury him; the burying is a further extension but entirely dependent upon my resolution. I submit that my resolution would be, so to speak, the senior motive in the situation.
I would direct attention to the fact that my resolution proposes that six months' notice should be given to the New Zealand government to cancel the treaty, whereas the language of the hon. gentleman is, that the order in council-naming it-shall be rescinded. But his proposed action to rescind would be of no effect whatever unless six months' notice was given under the treaty. I have the order in council before me, and it says that the provisions of the treaty, and so on, shall be "subject to the provisions of the said act." So you see the New Zealand arrangement comes under the Australian treaty and is "subject to the provisions of the said act." One of the provisions of the said act or treaty is that this government, if they wish to cancel the arrangement, must give six months' notice; and this provision therefore certainly applies to the New Zealand arrangement also. We cannot come along and say to New Zealand, "we rescind that order in council," and relieve ourselves of all obligation. If I grant a lease of my house to a man and the lease contains a covenant to give him six months' notice of my intention to terminate the tenancy, I cannot come along later and say, "I rescinded that lease some time ago, I regard it as no longer operative, and you must quit." He would say, "Well you may rescind that lease as much as you like, but I have my rights under that lease, and one of them is that I am entitled to six months' notice." If you tell the New Zealand government, "We have rescinded the order in council," they would say, "That does not matter to us, we want the six months' notice to which we are entitled." And the amendment of my hon. friend does not amount to anything unless the word "rescinding" means giving six months' notice. So in its spirit the amendment of my hon. friend embodies six months' notice. Therefore our two motions are practically the same, and I submit, sir, that I have established by the rules under which we are governed that my hon. friend's amendment is entirely out of order.
The word "relate" is very broad in its application and I leave it to the opinion of the house whether the motion moved by my hon. friend opposite does not relate to my resolution. The word "relate", I repeat, is very broad. I do not desire at this or any

There is no doubt as to what the terms of the amendment are as compared with the terms of the motion to which the hon. gentleman has referred. And there is another rule in England which Your Honour referred to on a previous occasion, that is, that the Speaker must be considerably governed by the general condition of the order paper and the likelihood of the matter being reached at an early day. In other words, there is a discretion given to the Speaker in a matter of this kind. In the cases to which reference is made in Maj', one was a bill standing upon the order paper for that evening. The motion is that the Speaker leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of supply. In amendment thereto Mr. Senn has moved, seconded by Mr. Rowe, that in the opinion of this house, order in council No. 1727, passed on 26th September, 1925, respecting certain treaty arrangements with the Dominion of New Zealand, should be rescinded forthwith and immediate steps taken to negotiate a treaty with that dominion on fair and equitable terms. On a point of order, Mr. Neill
states that he has a motion on the same lines, on the orders of the day, or on the notice paper, No. 21, which reads as follows:
That in the opinion of this house, six months' notice should be given to the New Zealand government to cancel the application to that country of the provisions of what is generally known as the Australian treaty.
I have listened to the authorities which have been quoted, particularly Bourinot, which is our guide. It is true that on page 420 Bourinot says:
The ordinary rules of debate are applicable on this occasion; for instance, a matter already decided by the house, or of which notice has been given, or which stands upon the orders of the day, cannot be discussed.
Turning to the preceding page, however, I find this general principle:
The order of the day for the house to go into committee of supply having been read, the Speaker will put the question "that I do now leave the chair."-
That is what I have done.
-the same question is always put whenever the house is to go into committee of supply, in order to afford ah opportunity to members to propose amendments. On this point it is observed by an eminent authority that the ancient constitutional doctrine that the redress of grievances is to ibe considered before the granting of supplies, is now represented by the practice of .permitting every description of amendment to be moved on the question for the Speaker leaving the chair, before going into committee of supply or ways and means. Upon other orders of the day, such amendments must be relevant, but here they are permitted to relate to every question upon which a member may desire to offer a motion.
I find below the dictum of Sir John A. Macdonald:
The right to consider grievances at this stage is one of the first principles of the British constitution. But the practice has been much abused in England, and the commons have more than once considered what means can be devised for limiting discussion.
One of the means for limiting discussion is precisely the principle invoked by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), that no one should anticipate a discussion of a question already on the notice paper, but in England under that rule authority has been given to the Speaker of the house to decide whether or not amendments, such as the present one, should be debated in sipite of a motion drafted along similar lines. Such motions in England are termed blocking motions. I do not wish to a,pply the term to the motion of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, because he has drafted it in good faith. The term "blocking motion" is applied in England on account of the abuse which has taken place in regard to them. If you

Australian Treaty-Speaker's Ruling
will read Redlich, one of the best authors, you will find at pages 221 and 222 of his third volume that even in England they fear the consequences of a ruling which might prevent discussion of matters of public importance, on the ground of anticipation. He cites a case which came to the attention of the house in the year 1900. Redlich says:
It soon became a common practice to put down "blocking notices" for this purpose. Perhaps the practice was never more severely strained than' in the session of 1900, when a member, at the beginning of the session, put down a notice of motion in general terms with reference to the conduct of the war in South Africa, and then sailed for Africa to take part in the war without fixing any day for his motion. It was held that the mere retention of this -notice on the order book prevented discussion of the terms of peace with the Boers on the motion for adjournment for the Easter' recess.
It was considered a great abuse-not of the rule, because there is no rule-but of the usages and customs of parliamentary government in England. I do not look upon the motion made by the hon. gentleman as a blocking motion. It is on the order paper, and no doubt the hon. gentleman intended to bring it to the attention of the house at the earliest opportune date, but there is a point which cannot be ignored. The two motions differ materially in one respect; I grant that the provision for six months' notice is in the treaty, and whether you mention it as regards the abrogation or cancellation of the treaty it matters not because the treaty cannot be cancelled without giving six months' notice. I think you will find that delay mentioned in almost every treaty. But there is this which, in my mind, shows that there is a material difference between the two motions:	The
motion of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni proposes simply the cancellation of the treaty after six months' notice; the other one proposes the rescission or cancellation forthwith and-mark this-that immediate steps be taken to negotiate a treaty with that dominion on fair and equitable terms. In the one case the hon. member for Comox-Alberni asks for cancellation of the treaty; in the other case it is being asked that the treaty be cancelled, but that immediate steps be taken to negotiate another treaty with that dominion on fair and equitable terms. As the rule of anticipation is, shall I say, strictissimi juris, I should give to the amendment a broad interpretation. The two motions differ materially and in my humble judgment the amendment is in order.
